Does the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, through the historic sites and monuments board of Canada, intend to build a monument to the memory of the patriots of 1837, either in St. Denis or St. Charles on the Richelieu river?

Answer: After having reviewed the various proposals submitted to the historic sites and monuments board of Canada in the last few years, I must say that no general proposal has been submitted to the board with a view to having erected a monument to the memory of the patriots of 1837, and that neither the department nor the board contemplates for the time being the possibility of erecting such a monument.

subtopic: TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING ASSISTANCE ACT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the resolution stage a number of questions were posed by hon. members on the opposite side of the house, and a number of statements were made. I wish to thank hon. members
Vocational Training Assistance Act for their contributions, and for their cooperation in getting the resolution through in what can be termed markedly short order.
The hon. member for Ontario, the former minister of labour, is a man for whom I have great admiration. He and I are probably among those members least qualified to be ministers of education; our alma mater would seem to be the school of hard knocks, and for this reason I have great affinity for the hon. member. I have been going through the Parliamentary Guide, and I notice that we have both received a great deal of our education since we found it necessary to make our own way in life.
However, this need not deter me from commenting on some of the points he raised. The hon. member took exception to my statement that this was an entirely new measure. If he will examine what I said he will find I was referring to a statement made by the Minister of Labour on June 10, at which time he put forward what he termed a new manpower development program. Some of it was entirely new, and other parts of it constituted an extension of the program already in existence.
The hon. gentleman took exception to the fact that the bill introduced in the previous session of parliament by himself with respect to manpower adjustment had not been revised. If that criticism were valid I think it could equally be said that it was unnecessary in 1961 for the government of that day to have brought in the technical and vocational training act because there was already in existence, as of 1942, the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act. There is not a great deal of difference between the two acts, and amendment would have sufficed. I am sure the hon. member will feel upon reflection that the introduction of amendments at this time to the technical and vocational training act is quite in order.
Aside from that, the hon. member made a constructive contribution, as did the hon. member for Medicine Hat, the hon. member for Kindersley, and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. The hon. member for Kindersley has obviously had a great deal of experience in the field of education and vocational training.
The hon. member for Quebec East made some statements, however, which I believe are not valid. If we reread them we will realize that the hon. member was speaking of the past and of the circumstances which prevailed before these amendments were introduced. He referred to the minister of youth for Quebec as having made certain statements suggesting that Quebec was not receiving its share under this program, and that the program discriminated against Quebec. Well, this

Vocational Training Assistance Act has no relation whatever to the facts. Mr. Gerin Lajoie, who is minister of youth in the province of Quebec, is also chairman of the provincial ministers who have met on occasion and who, at their most recent meeting, drafted a statement to the federal Minister of Labour asking specifically for the amendments which are contained in his measure. I should like to quote from that brief in order to demonstrate that this is a fact. The second last paragraph of the brief presented to the Minister of Labour by this committee says:
For the reasons here briefly set forth, we now believe that the national interest makes it imperative that the federal technical and vocational training act be amended so that the federal government's contribution in respect of capital expenditures incurred by the provinces be calculated at 75 per cent of all such expenditure made prior to the end of the agreement, the 31st March, 1967.
That is the essence of the amendments now before us though there are, of course, several other provisions having to do with the training aspects of the program.
I have a brief prepared statement which I should like to read to the house since hon. members now have the bill before them. I might say that I am unable to answer the question raised by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. I have not had an opportunity to discuss the matter he raised, but perhaps tomorrow on the orders of the day he may be able to have his question answered by putting it directly to the minister concerned.
The provisions of Bill No. C-105 reflect in detail the proposals announced in the house by the minister on June 10 and explained in more detail when the resolution was introduced on October 2. These measures are designed to further strengthen the federal-provincial program of manpower development and training, having particular application to the provision of suitable and adequate training facilities, the training of the unemployed, and encouraging the training of adult employed workers so they may adjust to changing employment conditions.
The first section of this bill provides that in respect of the costs incurred by a province in providing training allowances for unemployed persons, the maximum contribution payable by Canada be increased from 75 per cent to 90 per cent. As the minister pointed out on June 10, 1963 when he drew attention to the major feature of the government's employment and manpower development program, there was at that time the anomaly of high unemployment and a shortage of skills.
Last year training was provided by the provinces for 38,439 unemployed persons,


with the federal government contributing 75 per cent of both training costs and living allowances. This was an increase over the previous year's enrolment of approximately 43 per cent, but the program must be increased beyond last year's enrolment if it is to provide for those unemployed who would benefit from training. By increasing the federal contribution to living allowances while maintaining the 75 per cent contribution to direct training costs the provinces will be able to release more funds to support the additional training required. This program for the training of the unemployed is extremely important and must be expanded, but in the longer range it is equally important to provide upgrading and retraining programs for those employed persons who are in danger of becoming unemployed in the future. This then is the purpose of the second amendment.
In subsection 2 of section 1 provision is made for the federal government to contribute an additional 25 per cent of provincial costs in respect of certain programs for employed adults. The purpose of this amendment is to stimulate training in industry beyond the short range production requirements which heretofore have been the general pattern. This extra incentive will be directed to the longer range programs including upgrading of the general background of employed workers in mathematics, science and communications skills, and to the long term, organized development of skilled craftsmen through apprenticeship. It will also provide for the retraining of workers who are in imminent danger of lay-off because of technological changes in industry. It is not the intention of the government to relieve industry of its traditional responsibility for training its employees to meet production requirements, but rather to stimulate provinces to take a more active part in participating with and encouraging industry to undertake training programs that are in the national interest.
Although there has been expansion of the training facilities in excess of 144,000 student places, the development has been uneven among the provinces. Some were in a position to take very limited advantage of the provisions of the legislation. These variations ranged from $51 per capita in the 15-19 age group in Quebec to $480 in Newfoundland. The experience has shown that in spite of the increase in student places up to the present, the response on the part of the Canadian people has been such that even further increases are needed, especially in the provinces where lesser amounts have been claimed.

Section 2 of Bill No. C-105 provides for an extension of the period during which contributions payable by Canada for capital expenditures incurred by the provinces on technical and vocational training facilities will be 75 per cent of provincial government expenditure. The contribution will be continued at this level in each province until the $480 has been contributed on behalf of each person in the 15-19 age group or until March 31, 1967, whichever is earlier. After this time the federal contribution will be reduced to 50 per cent of provincial expenditures. This will allow provinces to share in the provisions for capital facilities to an equal extent, and will at the same time give more time to put these facilities in place. On this basis the amount which would be available to each province before the rate of contribution is reduced to 50 per cent of provincial expenditures would be as follows:

Section 3 provides for an increase in membership of the national technical and vocational training advisory council from 23 to 28 members. This increase in membership is intended to give greater representation on the council to representatives from industry, labour and other interested groups. Subsection 2 of section 3 of the bill provides for an honorarium for the chairman of this council. Because of the growing requirements on council for consideration of matters of national concern, the demands on the chairman are growing. It is therefore proposed to provide an honorarium.
After close study of the total manpower training needs the government feels that these amendments to the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act are required to meet adequately the training needs of Canada. I ask the house for a continuation of the co-operation already extended, and because the bill is so vital in the interests of the training of our youth and in the interests of all Canada, I hope it will be passed by the house as expeditiously as possible.

Question.
Vocational Training Assistance Act

subtopic: TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING ASSISTANCE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak I hear some of my colleagues opposite shouting "question". When we were at the resolution stage we were urged not to speak then in order to save time, and to leave our comments for second reading of the bill. I might tell some of my hon. friends opposite who represent farming constituencies that I intend to deal principally with the need of extending vocational training to the young farmers of this country. Apparently they are not interested in this problem.
I rise to support the principle and purpose of this most important piece of legislation, and to support the suggestions made by various speakers on behalf of this party who spoke at the resolution stage. However, this afternoon I wish to deal with one particular aspect of vocational training, namely vocational training in agriculture, for which there is a growing need in Canada.
I speak as one who has had a rather close association with agriculture and forestry all my life, and I have a great respect for the opinions of farmers and other rural people. I think everything possible should be done to assist the young people in our farming communities to carry on as successful farmers, succeeding their fathers in the days to come. I have heard this question discussed at meetings of farmers, fruit growers and people representing other types of agriculture; I have discussed it myself with a number of individuals including some of the educational authorities of British Columbia and with practical farmers, those who are particularly concerned with the application of this type of legislation to rural communities.
I suppose it is almost a truism to say that everyone interested in farming these days talks about the need of extending vocational training in agriculture, but very little has been done about it to date. As I see it, the main reason so little has been done about vocational training in agriculture is the many different opinions as to what is required to meet this need, and to some extent I have no hesitation in blaming some of the agricultural organizations who I think have failed to grasp the significance of this type of legislation until recent months. However, changing circumstances and growing awareness of the need are causing farmers' organizations to take a more positive approach to this problem. I think this is particularly so in the province of Saskatchewan and also in British Columbia.
Labour organizations and industrial and commercial leaders have already given active attention to this type of legislation and the problem it is supposed to meet, to ensure
4862	HOUSE OF
Vocational Training Assistance Act that in so far as is possible under the present economic system, vocational training will fill their future needs. However, to date the federal Department of Labour and the provincial departments of education have been given little guidance from farmers' organizations and educational groups with respect to the needs of extending vocational training in agriculture. I give full credit to the federal Department of Trade and Commerce for giving some leadership to industry in the use of vocational training grants, and some provinces have co-operated in analyzing the needs of industry and commerce.
I understand the federal Department of Labour, which is responsible for carrying out the terms of the Vocational Training Assistance Act, has attempted, in so far as federal jurisdiction is concerned, to pursue the same course in respect of agriculture. X hope the minister listens to what I have to say at this point, because I am trying to be my usual constructive self. I am advised that the Department of Labour made a survey of what was required in agricultural training in each province, and they used this information as the basis for discussion at a conference of agriculturists and educationalists that was later called in Ottawa. However, I am advised that with the exception of Saskatchewan the provinces carrying out this survey never sought the advice of practical farmers, but were content to limit their investigations or to obtain their advice from the educational authorities in the provinces concerned.
I do not wish to throw a shadow upon the ability of educational authorities, but in this particular field, when you come to deal with the practical problems related to agriculture which change so much from province to province, from region to region and from one type of agriculture to another, you cannot get sound advice by simply consulting educationalists. You must seek some advice from farmers' organizations and also from practical farmers. We must recognize the fact that the needs in agriculture are changing so rapidly it is difficult to assess them and plan a long term program. We all recognize that difficulty. Agriculture is faced in that respect with the same difficulty as other segments of the economy.
On the other hand, while our program so far as agriculture is concerned is practically in the embryo stage, we must recognize that 13 per cent of the farm labour force of the United States are now using vocational agricultural training facilities, while in Canada to date only 3 per cent of our farm labour force is doing so. There is a big contrast here which should spur us on to greater action.


Now, let us see what is being done in some of the provinces in this respect. I have not the full information, but I have some information from some of the provinces. I am advised that Ontario is offering ten 12-week courses in the fundamentals of maintaining and operating a farm. This is all to the good. I am advised that Quebec probably has the most comprehensive program operating on three levels. I am very taken with the result of my inquiries as to what is happening in Quebec. I am very pleased indeed to see it. I am informed that there are three institutions offering technical agricultural training, and 14 local school boards in Quebec have a good, comprehensive adult training program for men and women at the local level to meet their circumstances, to meet their needs, to meet their convenience and their pocketbooks.
In Manitoba I am advised that apart from the high school diploma agricultural institutes there are practical short courses of three or four days' duration given once per year over television between 10.30 and 12 o'clock, using a special network at low cost when these stations are usually off the air. This is one field that could be investigated and the same principle applied in other provinces. Saskatchewan, I am advised, among the many other aspects of its program, is offering a new two term course in farm machinery upkeep and repair. This is a very necessary course with the increased mechanization on our farms. I have repeatedly gone on farms and found operations at a standstill because no one on the farm could make a minor repair to a combine or some piece of machinery which is very complicated from my point of view. All my early farming days were spent with a walking plow, an axe, a cross-cut saw and a grub hoe. There is training needed in this field, and Saskatchewan is giving a lead in respect of the training of persons in the repair and upkeep of farm machinery.
I am very sorry to say, Mr. Speaker, that in British Columbia our record is rather poor. Out of a total farm labour force of 28,000 there were only 149 students attending day courses and 57 taking advantage of the night courses early this fall. However the agriculture occupational courses at the University of British Columbia are today using vocational training methods.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this could be interpreted as being the fault of too few locations for training in British Columbia, located too far away from prospective students and perhaps not providing the type of training the students want. I have heard that complaint made about the training program that is being undertaken at the moment. In my opinion British

Columbia should establish a permanent practical agricultural school farm giving two season practical courses available to people of all ages who have discontinued their formal education. This program could be interwoven with the vocational training assistance program. This is a very necessary program in respect of the training of young farmers and others who wish to further their training in agriculture in British Columbia.
There are a number of other alternatives I should like to mention, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps the simplest of these would be that both governments should share the cost and more modern and practical courses should be established. We should again encourage our school boards to make agriculture a positive course in rural high schools. I think there is room for considerable improvement in that respect. In conjunction with this, the school facilities and teachers should be available for night classes for adults and for young farmers who wish this additional training. I think that could be woven into this technical assistance program.
Another idea, Mr. Speaker, would be to leave it up to the department of education and the school boards to decide whether they wished agriculture as a vocational training course in their schools, or would like the assistance of the university extension service and government financial aid made available in each part of the province for three or four day courses, each covering one basic facet of agriculture at a time but all of them including accounting and a basic knowledge of soils and fertilizers. I mention these sorts of fringe aspects of technical training because they are all interwoven. I think there has to be a good deal more study given to such technical and vocational training for our young farmers.
However, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a special plea for further consideration on the part of the minister to the great need for agriculture vocational training in all its various aspects. I suggest the federal departments of labour and agriculture and their provincial counterparts should consult representative farm organizations across Canada and other related organizations, including the agriculture institute of Canada. In addition I suggest that the provincial governments should follow the example of Saskatchewan and seek the advice of practical farmers in various fields of agriculture under varying regional circumstances and conditions.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I again emphasize the need for greatly expanded vocational training in agriculture, and urge that every effort be made to meet this need as soon as possible as a result of co-operation among federal and provincial governments, organizations of various types and farmers. I would
Vocational Training Assistance Act say when it comes to something of this type I have great respect for the intelligence and common sense of the farmers of this country who, I am confident, would be ready to offer their wholehearted co-operation to the federal and provincial governments to make sure the young farmers of today have the opportunities they are entitled to under this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, before discussing the purposes of this bill I would like to take a little time of the house to extend to the minister, a colleague from Nova Scotia, my congratulations on the better than average job he has been doing since he took over this portfolio. I wish to tell him that we in Nova Scotia are proud of the job he is doing and proud of the fact that, as usual, Nova Scotia is holding up its end in the federal cabinet.
I might also say that as a minister from Nova Scotia he has used the good common sense Nova Scotians seem to be endowed with, in following the policies introduced by the previous minister, the hon. member for Ontario, and in realizing the merit inherent in the legislation that is now being amended.
I am sure that since he assumed the duties of a cabinet minister he has become aware of the fact that there is no magic formula for curing unemployment, and that the best method of effecting the cure that must be carried out is to see that our young people are properly trained and fully capable of entering the labour market, and that our older workers are retrained in a manner that will provide them with their own saleability from an employment point of view.
The minister has proposed four main amendments to the act. The first is to provide that the federal government's share of the cost of training allowances be increased from 75 per cent to 90 per cent. The second is to assist to a greater degree in the "training in industry" programs, by increasing the federal contribution from 50 per cent to 75 per cent of the costs. The third is to extend the period during which contributions payable by the federal government for capital expenditure incurred by the provinces on training facilities will be 75 per cent, and the fourth is to increase the size of the council from 23 to 28 members and to pay an honorarium to its chairman.
I find no objection whatsoever to the first three amendments, and I would just as soon leave the fourth one. There seems to be a growing tendency on the part of the government to increase the size of boards, but I find more can be accomplished with a smaller group of individuals than with a large group, and the effectiveness of a council is usually predicated on the number of individuals placed on it. However, I must say I am in
4864	HOUSE OF
Vocational Training Assistance Act full agreement with the amendments put forward and will certainly vote for them.
If the minister could assist in persuading his colleagues in the cabinet to extend family allowances he would help this program to an even greater degree, for it would allow people with families to keep their children in school longer so they could take advantage of this vocational training to an even greater extent.
Speaking in Newfoundland on November 12 the minister, among other things, stated:
Over 530 projects, designed to expand existing vocational schools or to establish new ones, have been approved since April 1, 1961-[DOT]
The total cost of the buildings and equipment alone will exceed $525,000,000. The federal government has agreed to contribute more than $330,000,000 toward this investment In Canada's future.
I agree with what he said, but I think he should have pointed out, without detracting in any way from his own contribution, that the hon. member for Ontario and the former government put this program on the road. They saw where the problem was and how it could be eliminated. They took the necessary action that today is bringing the rewards we are able to note in the fact that there are over 140,000 new students obtaining this type of technical and vocational training.
There is one matter I would like to raise regarding the calling of tenders for the construction of these institutions to which the government contributes 75 per cent of the cost. I bring it to the minister's attention in the hope something might be done to eliminate grievances that have been developing among certain subcontractors who are not receiving the type of protection that is available to them under the Department of Public Works.
In my constituency there are a number of firms which from time to time submit subtenders to prime contractors for projects of this type, but unfortunately, because the subcontractors do not receive the protection afforded by the Department of Public Works, they find that the prime contractors do either one of two things. An individual prime contractor has either used the subtender, after a contract has been awarded, as a method for renegotiation to force the subcontractor down in his price if he wishes to carry out the work, or the prime contractor has listened to the government of the province, in this case New Brunswick, and has ignored a subcontractor who happens to come from Nova Scotia. This is a result of interference from the government of New Brunswick, and in one case a firm that should have carried out the work was completely eliminated from the job, although unfortunately it was kind enough to provide the prime contractor with


the price on which he made his bid and which allowed him to secure the contract.
I realize that the amount of interference the federal government should exercise in the field of education is a matter of some concern to some provinces. However, when the federal government is putting up 75 per cent of the cash I think it has a right to request that certain things be done, and done in a proper manner. In this respect one particular firm, which to my knowledge lost at least two contracts, has been treated unfairly. I do not think the taxpayer has been treated fairly, and I believe the federal government has the right to and should demand protection for all subcontractors who submit bids on these projects. Certainly if this had been the case there would have been more employment in my constituency, and more employment for this very competent firm.
There is also the fact that if this program is continued-and there is every indication that it will be-we will restore a degree of confidence in our unemployed citizens that they did not have before we brought this program into being in 1961. It has been very noticeable in the town of Springhill in my constituency that men who are without jobs and the means of securing employment because of lack of training very quickly become despondent and are not capable of making the full contribution they once did. This retraining of older workers, especially at the higher rates that we put into effect, makes new men out of older men. It gives them a new hope and a new determination, and it makes Canada a better place in which to live.
Anything we as a government can do to improve the education of our people is of great importance to all Canadians. Certainly the investment we are making with regard to this program is tremendous. I think the results are tremendous also. I believe we will have a more qualified working force because of it. However, I think we must take further steps, such as those mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West in the field of agriculture. There is still a need to provide a greater degree of training in this field where technology has taken over, perhaps not as noticeably as in the field of industry but to the same significant degree. Anything that can be done to interest our young people in agriculture to a greater degree, and better train them so that when they enter work in this field they are of more value to those who employ them, will be of benefit to the Canadian nation. I recommend to the minister that he give very careful consideration to the recommendations made by the hon. member for Kootenay West.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude by urging the minister to work as hard as he can to convince his colleagues in the cabinet that family allowances should be extended at the earliest possible date, so that parents who are considering what they should do regarding the further education of their children might decide to take advantage of the numerous vocational schools that have been built by the Stanfield government in my province and by other governments in the other provinces of Canada. These parents would be given the security that is available with even this small cheque each month. I would also ask the minister to see that the subcontractors who are submitting tenders to prime contractors for the construction of these institutions are given the protection that they deserve and should have, for it is neither right nor proper that federal funds should be used by a provincial government to discriminate against firms because they happen to be located in one province, whereas the work is being done in another.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to unduly spin out this discussion, but I feel I would be remiss if I did not make some observations at this stage of the bill.
My first remarks will be to commend the minister for having revised and reconsidered this legislation in order to meet at least the representations expressed last spring by the minister of education of the province of Quebec who called for an extension of the act so that our province could take advantage of it at least until 1967.
I do not intend to recall here all the disadvantages entailed by this act the day it was passed by the federal government. From an educational standpoint, several provinces, like the province of Ontario, were then ready to take advantage of the act. But statistics show that the province of Quebec did not fully profit from it.
I also commend him for having thought of making an adjustment in the per capita grants for the students in the 15-19 age group who, in the province of Quebec, will attend high schools, technical schools and trade schools. This adjustment will more adequately equalize the technical and vocational training all across the country.
I should like to recall here some of the principles at the basis of those representations. At the beginning, when the legislation was introduced, accepted and passed by parliament, I think that the majority intended to facilitate that technical training needed by our young people and, at the same time, provide some assistance for the recipients of
Vocational Training Assistance Act those benefits during a period of seasonal unemployment. In brief, those who were completely without means were given allowances while acquiring a better technical or vocational training in the trades already carried out by those older people.
However, I feel that in some cases that training did not turn out exactly as it was expected at the time the legislation was enacted. In fact, I remember certain cases in my riding where this legislation was not a happy experience for young people of 20 to 30 years of age.
Under the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act, those young unemployed were taken on a free bus ride of 20, 25 or 30 miles each morning, in winter, to the Beauce-ville armouries where they were given a certain training.
The first week of the course was somewhat similar to the period when we used to pass our military tests. For a week endeavours were made to find out the aptitudes of the students.
During the second week, training in first aid was about all they got; for a whole week, they received stretcher bearer and hospital orderly courses.
During the third week, they were taught the meaning of some signs on the uniforms of service men in this country; what the stripes on the sleeves mean: if there are two it is a lance corporal; if there are three, it is a sergeant. That was during the third week.
At the end of the fourth week, the teachers tried to stress the advantages of voluntarily enlisting in the army for a period of three years, since the students were out of a job.
That was all there was at the time, to the so-called "technical training" of hundreds of young people in our province. It seems to me that such methods are, to some extent, along the lines of the philosophy expounded the other day by the hon. member for Beau-harnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel), that is, that the best way to train our young people is to have them undergo compulsory military service.
I feel that there should be other means of giving technical and vocational training to young people. We have, in the province of Quebec, as well as in other provinces, numerous institutions which might, through the instrumentality of the law, offer technical and vocational training to our leaders of tomorrow. In so doing, we would work in the best interest of our fellow countrymen of today and of tomorrow.
I wished to make these few remarks, in the hope that the present type of training might be discontinued, at least in the province of Quebec. I have also noticed that in the province of Quebec the act discourages those

Vocational Training Assistance Act who should have priority in matters of education or who would derive the greatest benefits from a refresher course in their own field.
Here again, I believe that this legislation does not meet completely the requirements of certain trades.
For instance, let us think for a moment of the train of thoughts of a person 45, 48 or 50 years old who, for 25 or 30 years, has been a house painter and who faces unemployment due to the winter season. He is then invited to attend refresher courses. And often, the instructors are young 22 or 23 year old men who never painted an 8 by 4 wallboard, whilst the students, as it were, are persons who practised their trade for 30 years.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that, under such circumstances, the people do not get a very high idea of how public funds are spent for vocational training purposes.
However, X would not like my remarks to be construed as to mean that I am not in favour of this improvement in the field of vocational training.
On the other hand, in the province of Quebec, together with representatives of the federal Department of Labour, employers and the officials of certain union groups, we have carried out experiments and designed a method of improvement and education for workers in industry and the trades which proved perhaps more efficient than that to which I referred previously in connection with various trades.
Mr. Speaker, when the act was passed in 1961, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) took part on two or three occasions in the discussion on that legislation which seemed badly needed in this country. However, going through his remarks, I did not find any reference to the fact that this legislation is a direct interference in an exclusively provincial field. On the other hand, the member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) referred to this fact. As for us we have strongly objected to the interferences of the federal government in a field which was and still is, according to our constitution, exclusively reserved to the provinces.
In this connection, I should like to quote an editorial which appeared in Le Devoir of February 18, 1963 and reads as follows:
This claim made by Quebec is all the more legitimate as the funds given by Ottawa for vocational training belong to the provinces. The long term aim of a dynamic government must be to hand back to the provinces the funds which Ottawa grabbed under cover of war and the endless state of emergency which followed.
But until fair agreements have succeeded in fully restoring the spirit of the confederation act, we would in no way be justified in permitting that other provinces than Quebec spend a great part of the amounts that we pay ourselves into the federal treasury.

If the present situation should last, the provocation referred to by Mr. Gerin-Lajoie would result sooner or later in serious consequences for the future of the country.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not discuss the matter any further, but I am confident that hon. members will take those claims into account and that those who will take part in the next federal-provincial conference will better understand our position that may seem uncompromising to those who are not familiar with the problems of the province of Quebec.
Lately, we have heard a fair number of speeches concerning the withdrawal of joint programs in certain fields of economic activity in our country.
Mr. Speaker, I do hope that, in dealing with the measure now before us, we shall not forget that the province of Quebec does not wish to interfere in any way with normal development in the field of science or technology or with progress in any occupational area whatever, and that on a national scale, but it wants to be treated fairly when making claims which it believes to be reasonable and just.
That point of view must be taken into account, and especially in the way those courses are offered. Help is given to improve the knowledge of those who have had a trade or occupation for a good many years or of young people of 20 to 30 years of age who go and take technical or vocational training, in spite of the deficiencies I mentioned a while ago, a training which is very much similar to a military service training and where there was not even the slightest hesitation in handing out to the students-and free, if you please- khaki uniforms used by the armed forces of our country.
Mr. Speaker, that is further proof of the fact that Quebec is right in claiming those amounts which, if they are due to the province, should be paid back to it through its department of youth. Thus, when the legislation is finally adopted, the training would correspond to the aspirations of those youth and meet the standards of our system of education instead of consisting in rather strange technical courses for the training of people between the ages of 20 and 30.
Mr. Speaker, those are some of the remarks I wanted to make. I have no intention of repeating the figures quoted last week by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Beaule) but, for the information of my fellow citizens of the province of Quebec and other provinces who are interested in this problem, I should like to point out the discrimination which took place in the past under this legislation.
It will be realized, in the other provinces, that they are not being treated unfairly if, in the next three years, the province of Quebec

seems to get an amount of approximately $254 million, while Ontario will only be getting $9 million, Alberta $48 million and British Columbia $54 million.
I think that it is simply the result of the fact that we were not ready or that our education system in high schools and technical schools, under the direction of the board of education, did not meet the legal requirements, at that time.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that these few remarks will be taken in serious consideration during the next federal-provincial conference so that there will be a better understanding, in the end, of the Quebec position and its claims. I hope that this is not merely a case of political balloon to which one government or another may resort, at any level whatsoever, during an election campaign.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should also take steps to ensure that the country will be able to make a maximum use of the nation's vital forces. I have here the report issued following a survey conducted by the "J.O.C." in the province of Quebec, in 1960. Very interesting statistics have been disclosed as well as some discouraging ones.
For instance, a survey carried out in regard to 1958 and 1959 graduates of the various professional schools and technical institutes in the city of Quebec alone, showed that out of a total of 94 graduates having sent answers 42 were engaged in the trade they had learned, 33 had jobs but outside their trade and 19 were unemployed.
Now, that happened a year or two after they had left our own institutions where they had studied for 10, 12 or 15 years.
As for the situation in the city of Three Rivers, an ideal industrial location, according to what is said in the province of Quebec, out of 76 graduating students who replied', 20 were doing what they had studied for, 20 had jobs having nothing to do with their trade and 36 were unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, I think there are gaps not only at the technical and vocational training stage, but also at the formal education level.
The survey that was made shows that, out of 265 answers which were received, 88 persons or 33 per cent were practising the trade that they had learned; 104 or 39 per cent had jobs unrelated to their craft; the unemployed numbered 73 or 27 per cent.
Those figures prove that the gap is not only to be found at the educational level, because, Mr. Speaker, between a well-educated unemployed and a less-educated one, the problem remains the same.
We wish more and more to allow our young people to train to meet the requirements of

I feel that the deficiencies regarding this disastrous period of unemployment at home should be seriously considered together with technical and professional training.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to drag on this debate, but I am convinced these few remarks concerning the moneys which by right belong to the province of Quebec will be taken into consideration. As I said, I think that a very large part of the Quebec people wish to see that field, which is properly theirs, belonging to them and remaining theirs, according to standards already established and legislation already recognized by the very spirit of the confederation act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have an opportunity of taking part in the discussion of this technical and vocational training scheme.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the present world is in such rapid evolution that some sort of intellectual revolution is called for, among our young people as well as among the adults. Formerly, one could for instance, get along after a period of working as an apprentice with a man who thoroughly knew his trade. Moreover, a few years of elementary schooling were good enough for most people to succeed in life. For a large number of young people, especially in rural districts, elementary schooling consisted in a few years spent at school while waiting to be sturdy enough to work. Also, the greatest number were able to secure permanent employment where no particular training was required.
But, particularly in the last few years, applied science has upset our way of life. Automation added to an industrialization which is developing at a pace unknown before especially in Quebec in the last few years has taken us unaware. And that is why we see in every district which did not manage to become industrialized at the same rapid rate, the proportion of unemployment is extremely high, and even where industries are in full development, we have to face another major problem in the lack of trained workers and technicians needed for the operation of those industries. That is quite obvious in the province of Quebec in particular.
We were taken by surprise by this technological revolution, and the present government is doing what it can to remedy the situation.
I am sure that this bill will provide both long term and short term solutions by making possible the technical training of adults, but especially of the younger generation.

subtopic: TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING ASSISTANCE ACT

speechtext:
Let
me say at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, that I regard our vocational and technical training program as one of the most progressive steps forward in our fight against unemployment. When a Progressive Conservative government introduced this far reaching program back in December, 1960, it had as its intent not only fighting unemployment, but its main purpose was to plan for our future needs and head off unemployment. My friend, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis), said at the time the legislation was introduced that anyone who had studied the bill would have to admit it was the most positive step forward in the training field ever taken in this country. So say we all.
The impact of this program in three short years has been tremendous. When we left office in May of this year, the building program had approached the $450 million 28902-5-3104
Vocational Training Assistance Act level. Of this total, the federal government had contributed 75 per cent or, in other words, an investment by the federal government of $340 million in the training of skilled manpower and human resources. I am pleased to see that the present government is following along the path we blazed for it. However, last week in St. John's, Newfoundland, the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) reported that the program was now at the $525 million mark and that facilities had been made available to train 140,000 new students each year. I am amazed, however, at the bland and nonchalant statements contained in the minister's speech. Not one word does he devote to the history of the vocational and technical training school program. In other words, he would lead his audience and other listeners to believe that all this came from big daddy. However, on a subject as important as this, I do not want to drag the debate into a partisan arena.
I should like to say that I am entirely in favour of the program which, to date, has been a resounding success. I heartily commend the present government for its vision for continuing our program, and I hope that those provinces which have not participated as fully as they might will now take advantage of the opportunity to do so. It is now evident that the expanded technical and vocational training program promoted by our former minister of labour and the then government will have a beneficial effect on the whole educational system. Furthermore, other countries have shown an interest in the happenings in this field of development because it is obvious that the former government made great progress. Most important, Canadians have a new interest in education and appreciate as never before the importance of proper preparation for careers and the need to keep abreast of the times-yes, ahead of the times.
In my own riding, four projects were undertaken. The total cost of these improvements was over $2.6 million, and the federal government's share amounted to almost $2 million. Training facilities were provided for more than 1,100 students. It has been my pleasure to visit most of these buildings and I am certainly very much impressed by what is taking place. Before closing, I should like to point out that our government took the trouble to clear these arrangements with the provinces. All applications originated with the municipalities and there was a close accord and harmony between the federal government, the provinces and the municipalities. A word to the wise, I believe, is sufficient.

subtopic: TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING ASSISTANCE ACT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two parliaments ago when this legislation was initially introduced my colleague at that time, the hon. member tor Peterborough, Mr. Pitman, and I were critical of some aspects of the legislation, although we supported it. I should like to go into the justification for that criticism, which I think is still relevant. I do not believe these amendments meet it, and I do not suppose they were intended to do so.
The criticism that we put forward at that time really related to the fact that the legislation, because it did not fall within any kind of framework or plan, was not going to meet what most of us, and the minister, put forward as the justification for it, that is that this was going to be a measure that would provide Canada with the kind of plan and facilities and teaching set-up that would enable us to tackle the problem of the unemployed who were short of qualifications. I was interested in the good speech the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) made, in which he said, as reported at page 4729 of Hansard, that in the time he was responsible for this particular measure a total of 519 projects were completed, including 254 new schools, 4 technical institutions and 47 trade schools, providing space for some 138,000 students each and every year.
Now, let us look at those figures again. There were 254 new schools, 4 technical institutes and 47 trade schools. In other words, the major point that we made initially still holds good. I think the pattern which has developed since the new government took over would support the statement that by far the overwhelming proportion of building that has taken place has been for institutions that fit into the secondary school framework, and not for technical institutes and trade schools which are primarily the kind of institutions which will meet the problem of retraining the unemployed worker who is having difficulty with both his mobility and finding the kind of job to suit his talents.
This point is to me perhaps the most important one in underlining some of the gaps that still exist in our national educational program. It is probably true that the constituency of Port Arthur gained more per capita out of this legislation than any other constituency in Canada. I know a big vocational school is being opened there this coming Saturday, the Grom Morgan school in Port Arthur, and the parliamentary secretary was up in Port Arthur not too many months ago for the opening of another new school. There have also been many extensions to school buildings and a new composite high school down in Geraldton.
In my riding, and in my province, one of the consequences of this legislation is that we have had this marvellous upsurge in plant, but we are no nearer having a coherent program for advanced technical education, or for retraining people in the labour force who are having difficulties meeting the requirements of employers in that labour force, than we were several years ago.
There is no doubt we have an excellent building program. I can understand the authorities in Quebec, in their complaints and bleats which have led to one part of this legislation, that is, the extension of the time limit, because it was quite obvious Quebec was not ready, and misunderstood the intent of the original act. I have seen statements by Mr. Rene Levesque and Mr. Gerin Lajoie to the effect that they misunderstood the intention of the legislation, that it was primarily in the technical institutions and trade school field, but that instead they discovered it was taken up by Ontario and British Columbia as a means of meeting the cost of a great new secondary school building program.
I think we ought to be realistic and admit that out of the act so far we have got a magnificent contribution on the part of the federal government and the provinces that responded to the problem of providing the country with more secondary schools. I insist the program has not really met head on the problem of retraining the older worker, the unemployed worker. The responsibility for this particular challenge is still resting with the local boards of education, many of which are having difficulty meeting it, not only in terms of funds but in finding the teachers and in meshing in a real training program for the older workers in this kind of school plant created as a result of the act, which plant is primarily being used for secondary school purposes.
We have had a lot of well wishing with regard to this legislation, and the idea that it is going to give great opportunity to our young people to have technical and vocational education. We have heard it said that there should be no stigma attached to this kind of education, and that we need more of it. Admittedly this is so, but in essence the new technical schools and vocational schools we have in Ontario are fulfilling merely part of the secondary school program, which I insist is not principally a training for a specific job or for the development of greater skills within this particular age group that will enable them to go right out into the work force.
All that the government has done in providing secondary school places is fine, but it is still not meeting the other challenge. One of the disappointments in this respect is

that the legislation merely consists of three parts which are important. I do not think the last part, dealing with the honorarium and expansion of the council is vital, but the other three parts are important.
The first is that maximum contribution for training allowances for unemployed persons has been raised from 75 per cent to 90 per cent. This is excellent. This is one contribution that will certainly help the local school boards in meeting the cost. The other amendment, increasing the contribution from 50 per cent to 75 per cent of the cost to the provinces for those people being trained in "training in industry" programs, is also excellent; but again neither of these two important items is really going to meet the fact that we have not a coherent national program in this field.
I think I can make this point best from an article by J. B. St. John which appeared in the Globe and Mail on March 22, 1963, entitled "Money now, a plan later." It reads:
A country caught up in the technological age inevitably faces new and profoundly complex educational problems. The issues of technical education and training for skill do not challenge the principles of the humanist education, but they force an accommodation and a measure of adjustment. In our kind of society, it is not any longer a question of either a cultural education or a technical education, but rather that both are necessary.
In a simpler society, 200 years ago and more, there were only a few occupations, dominated by agriculture and to some extent by commerce. Most of these forms of work were learned at home, or by apprenticeship or indenture arranged by the home.
After the rise of the industrial revolution, with its machines and impersonal factories, the old methods of learning occupations began to break down. Apprenticeship survived for a time in certain types of skilled jobs. But the refusal of many employers to accept the responsibility and expense of training apprentices created the idea of the technical school to fill the gap. The first of these began to appear in Europe and elsewhere around 1890.
There was a considerable interest in technical education in Canada mainly in the first decade of this century, and following the first world war. The purpose of technical schools was misconceived, however, and they were used as dumping grounds for the academically slow, and after a comparatively small number of technical schools had been built, interest virtually died among the public and in the higher levels of official education.
I think I might divert here to say I agree with this analysis completely because I followed the royal commission on technical education after the first world war, and have seen the developments in Ontario where, during the early twenties and mid-twenties there was this spirited upsurge of technical schools, which failed very largely in their purpose because they did become dumping grounds. The article continues:
Today, nobody could call our society simple. There are thousands of occupations ranging from inexpressibly difficult intellectual work down to the most menial and repetitive of jobs. But the
Vocational Training Assistance Act
dominant fact of modem life in Canada is that technology has destroyed many basic forms of work for good, and this has left people lacking an adequate education virtually unemployable. Also, the special skills needed in industry we have tended to import, instead of training our own people. These outside sources are becoming unavailable. Our indifference to technical education has produced a crisis.
The dominion Department of Labour has been struggling since the war to rouse some interest in a broad pattern of technical education in Canada. Rehabilitation, vocational programs, trade training and the like, have been the subject of many conferences, but the effort has not caught the public ear. It was only when a block-buster approach of an enormous grant for building technical schools, trade schools and other types, offered by the dominion government, was tried that the provinces came to life, and grabbed the money while it was going. Plans came afterward.
The block-buster referred to here was the act introduced by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) when he was minister of labour. Mr. St. John goes on:
How far short we are in this country of having a well co-ordinated, thoroughly planned technical training program is evident from the details of the speech by C. Ross Ford, federal director of vocational training, to the conference on education, concluded in this space yesterday. It should be emphasized that Mr. Ford's intention was factual, not critical, but any inference that may be made from this remarkable catalogue of other countries' programs only underlines the woeful inadequacy of what we are doing.
Technical training on all its levels, is not just a matter of schools, teachers and a course of study. It involves a close and active liaison between the school system, employers, unions, parents, young people and adults. It requires the definition of standards of training, co-ordinated examination levels, a clear understanding of the various forms and purposes of technical education.
It also involves the elimination of overlapping and wasted facilities, the abandonment of outdated restrictions, such as the provision that people over 21 cannot be taught elementary subjects in school. It requires the acceptance of school training on an appropriate level, as a substitute for or alternative to traditional forms of apprenticeship. There must be an elimination of restricted admission to some occupations, in view of the huge social necessity for employment opportunities for the millions of post-war young people.
It is a pity that there was not a proper recognition of the foundations for a national technical training program before the financial inducement was offered.
The remark made at the first Canadian conference on education that "there is nothing much wrong with Canadian education that a great deal of money, properly applied, would not set right", is largely fallacious. We do need money, but far more than money we need thoughtful planning, a huge degree of persuasion and public enlightenment and, most of all, an understanding of the structure, mentality and needs of Canadian society.
Then this is the concluding paragraph that puts the thing in focus to me:
Here in Ontario we plunged headlong into an incredible spending spree for technical high schools and additions, amounting all told, if the politicians are to be believed, to nearly $200 million, and we had no plan beforehand. It may not be too late to start.

Vocational Training Assistance Act
I do not know whether there is any plan, but I do know that the school boards which have gone for these new schools are getting caught up in the higher cost of the technical and vocational programming that follows from the building. Mr. S. J. Rendall, who is prominent in the Ontario department of education, revealed that technical and commercial courses add 30 per cent to school bills:
Vocational classes have 20 pupils, on average, compared with 30 in academic courses, putting teacher salary costs higher.
To claims that in metro Toronto vocational classes cost twice as much to operate, Mr. Rendall said metro school boards write off much of their night school costs in day pupils, distorting the school boards' statistics.
Ontario, with only 430 high schools of all types, is building 225 new projects under the vocational training scheme agreed on in 1960 by the two senior governments.
That is from the Toronto Star of March 22, 1962. I make this point because there is no provision in this bill for a higher contribution toward these built-up costs that will go to the school boards now dealing with and working in these plans. I think that is a criticism of the bill that can well be made. I think that because these added costs hit the school boards they should receive a larger contribution from the federal government on a continuing basis. I do not know why the government hesitated to do this. I do not know whether it was because of the stock fear that all of us have when we hear the screams from the Quebecers; but it does seem to me this is something that will have to be brought within this program if it is going to be national in scope.
I want to turn to something that is much more current than Mr. St. John's analysis of a year ago. This is the brief that was presented just the other day by the Canadian teachers federation to the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, Prime Minister of Canada. This is an excellent brief which really sets out to analyse the situation in Canada with regard to education, and equality of opportunity for education. I think it is a brief that all hon. members should read. I would particularly recommend it to our friends in Quebec who are so anxious to get everything in education within their own province and not have the federal government contributing at all. Some of the statistics, both in terms of the amount of money that Quebec is actually spending for education and the percentage of dropouts in Quebec, are likely to shock them. One of the conclusions to which I came - after looking at the statistics was that Quebec, like many of the other provinces, certainly needs to do something desperately about its education. I still remain unconvinced, having heard the arguments, particularly from

over here on my left, that the way it should do it is by cutting itself off completely from any relationship to a national plan or national objectives, and in doing this probably scuppering or destroying the intention and the wish of most of the rest of the country to have a national plan and some kind of national framework in this particular field. The Canadian teachers federation says this:
We intend to state our conviction that this is not merely a provincial problem, but a national one.
I will repeat that for the hon. member from Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin). This is what the Canadian teachers federation says:
We intend to state our conviction that this is not merely a provincial problem, but a national one.
They continue:
It is not one that might quietly fade with the passage of time, but one that is increasing in urgency. Nor is it merely an emotional argument. It is one that is logical, and based on the knowledge that education has a direct relationship to a nation's economic growth.
I would like to suggest to the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabasca, and other members in this house who have expressed similar views to his, that if he would accept this argument of national economic growth I think he would have to agree that this national economic growth is indivisible in terms of Quebec or the rest of the country. But there is another point in this connection. I want to conclude that part dealing with the analysis of the problem, and the urgency, and come down to this. On page 2 the brief says:
Canada has long since reached a state of national emergency in education. Educational costs are expected to double in the next decade. The post-war boom in enrolment has not levelled off: indeed the ratio of young children to the rest of the population has been increasing rapidly. Even the practical matter of unemployment is affected more by the general level of education than by limited, short term measures such as the Technical and Vocational Training Act.
In other words, the teachers federation of Canada has come to the conclusion that this particular measure is a limited, short term one. This is the basic criticism that we advanced about this program several years ago and it is one that I repeat here: it is a limited, short term program. I would like an answer from the minister or his parliamentary secretary-a candid answer-as to whether the government intends to make this more than a limited, short term program. I would like to know what answer they are going to give such an analysis by the Canadian teachers federation of this particular program. In the candid answer that I hope the minister will give I would like him to present us with an analysis of what factors apply in the government's thinking at this time. The factor

I want to hear about is whether all these screams, yells and howls from Quebec in connection with such program may be the reasons, or may be associated with the reasons, for the government and the minister not going forward with something that is long term and embracing. The brief continues:
Measures in any one field can never be satisfactory if built upon an unstable base. Additional training or retraining for jobs requiring technical skills cannot be effective unless those being trained have an adequate basic education. It is at this level-the provision of a generally high quality of basic education-that the problem continues in ever increasing magnitude.
The brief then goes into some of the indicators of inequality. The arguments and statistics in this brief bowl one over when you realize just how unequal are educational opportunities in Canada, both in terms of the proportion of teachers and the retention rates at the junior matriculation level by provinces.
I think members from Alberta should be proud of the fact that their province has a 60 per cent retention rate at the junior matriculation level. This goes away down; the bottom rate is for Quebec, 18 per cent amongst the Catholic schools in that province. The Protestant schools in Quebec have a somewhat better record of a 34 per cent retention. The brief goes into the reasons for inequality in terms of the basic wealth that is available to the provinces and the amount of effort the provinces could make.
The conclusion that you come to-at least, that I have come to, and I am sure anyone who looks at this brief closely will reach the same conclusion-is that we desperately need an equality of educational opportunity in this country, and we cannot do it as long as there is one part of the country that says no, or withdraws itself and insists that the other nine parts, in terms of provinces, have to accept the same basic attitude. I do not know what may be the solution to the particular dilemma that we face in this regard, but I do know this.
I am convinced that English speaking Canadians want a national program in a field such as this. They will support wholeheartedly the argument put forward in this brief; and if that means that this approach is unacceptable to the people of Quebec, then in this very important field it seems to me we ought to do what they ask, and that is to have a federal-provincial conference specifically on this question so that we can see where we stand, can get the lines drawn, and know who on the one hand are going to co-operate and accept or ask for leadership and contributions from the federal government, and who on the other hand are going to go along the line of running things
Vocational Training Assistance Act on their own. I am convinced that the magnitude both of the problem implicit in this act and in the whole educational picture is such that it has to be met on a national basis with a national effort.
If we are truly two nations-I am sure I can speak with more confidence on this than on anything else I may have sounded off about or gone out on a limb on-I am convinced that English speaking Canada wants such a national program, and that they will respond to the kind of arguments and requests put forward by the Canadian teachers federation. I think all these arguments and points put forward by the Canadian teachers federation are germane to this particular piece of legislation before us, and if the Prime Minister pays attention to this brief and sets up this kind of federal-provincial conference, which seems to me both timely and necessary, then before too many months have passed we will have the act back here with a much grander scope and with greater objectives to meet the national purpose.
