INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL LOCATION COUNCIL
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the establishment of a national location of industry council for the purpose of directing new industry into those regions of the country which are dependent on a narrow industrial base and those which are areas of surplus manpower; and empowering the national location of industry council, in co-operation with the monetary and fiscal authorities, to offer incentives to attract new industry to such regions when requested by provincial and municipal governments.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving this resolution this afternoon I am very concerned, as is the government, with areas which are not receiving their fair share of national development. It has recently been said in this house, and rightly so, that many of the areas now falling behind in industrial development are very much concerned at their being designated depressed areas. The area I represent is not a depressed area but one that has certainly lagged far behind the national trend of industrial development. I believe this question is something to which the federal government must give immediate consideration.


There are those, I am sure, who would say that the development of industry is not necessarily a responsibility of the federal government but that it should be left to free enterprise. However, the people of Canada have proven, over the years, that they do wish to do something to help certain types of industry, such as the gold mining industry, in particular circumstances. They have indicated this to the extent of a large portion of the $120 million which has been paid in cost aid to the gold mining communities over the last 16 years. Recently, within the last month, representatives of the gold mining communities came to Ottawa and presented a brief to the federal government in connection with the extension of emergency assistance. Those who are familiar with that presentation will be aware that many, though not all, of those communities had accepted cost aid as something of a permanent nature. Many of them, including the town of Timmins, had accepted it as the solution to the difficulties now being encountered by those communities. Others, including the township of Teck, believe that this form of assistance had not proved the answer to those difficulties. They do not believe it provides a future for the townships concerned and, in their view, it is only a means of maintaining an industry which could not otherwise survive. It is argued that the federal government, instead of raising the price of gold, or negotiating an increased price for that commodity, has preferred to give assistance to the mining communities, and that this alone has enabled them to survive for the last 16 years.
Because of the way in which this primary industry, of such great importance to Canada, has developed, I believe the day should never come when these communities are left to -their own resources unless, of course, the situation has radically changed. Some will say that the federal government ought not to involve itself in the community affairs of a particular area. However, we are already doing this, in a sense, by the assistance which is now provided to the designated areas. We have done it, too, in the Atlantic area by the creation of the Atlantic development board and the attempts made -to develop new industry in that area. I believe the time has come to give consideration to the needs of other areas in this nation. I have in mind, particularly, the gold mining industry which, it seems to me, can count on no future unless it has the support of provincial and federal governments, and unless the efforts of government at the local level are supported by the presence of new and diverse industries.
I am sure all members are well aware of the contribution which was made by this

industry to the national welfare in the 'thirties, especially, when this country was suffering from the effects of the depression. Many men from other parts of the country came to northern Ontario to work in the gold mines which were then enjoying a relatively prosperous period in relation to other industries. Many of the industries which were then established in the province of Ontario depended upon wealth being produced by the gold mines for their own livelihood. The prosperity of the gold mining industry was a stimulus to the economy of the entire nation. However, these mining communities are now reaching the end of their natural development and there is a need to provide them with assistance in new ways. By the phrase relocation of industry we do not mean taking industry out of one community and moving it to another. We mean that the federal government should provide incentives to encourage industries to enter Canada, or the province of Ontario, in which I am of course most interested, and establish themselves permanently. Possibly special incentives could be given with respect to areas where a certain percentage of the mines are in decline, or where a certain number of mines have been closed down. No doubt, if assistance of this kind were given, industry would be encouraged to enter such areas.
Action along these lines has been taken in Great Britain, though for a different reason. It was found that the facilities available in the traditional industrial areas were heavily overtaxed-there were not enough school houses or services of a municipal nature to allow the addition of substantial new industry in those areas. On the other hand, there were areas, such as we have in Canada, where there was a surplus of manpower and community resources readily available, though the latter could only be used to advantage if industry chose to settle in those districts. Anyone who travels to Britain today and examines the industrial development which has taken place in the north of that country, a region which 20 years ago depended primarily on the shipping industry and on mining, will be surprised at the facilities which have been provided, and the way in which declining industries have been replaced by young and vigorous new enterprises.
It is true that in Britain the government finds itself able to exercise a degree of control which the Canadian government is not yet, and may never be, in a position to use unless the tax relationship between the central government and the provincial governments is radically changed. In the United Kingdom the government is able to decide what concessions shall be made to attract industries to locate in any given area. It is also able to influence the 28902-5-311
National Location of Industry Council decision whether or not a company may raise the finances necessary to expand or locate in a given area. We may not be in such a position here in Canada, but I do believe there are incentives which could be granted so as to encourage development wherever it was thought desirable to do so. There is no area in Canada which does not possess certain advantages. All areas have assets which could be taken into account by any federal government which wished to provide the machinery necessary to assist them.
I am sure the Department of Industry is going to do this for Canada as soon as it has the facilities available. This is a new department, and I am pleased to note that some of the up to date councillors of the township of Teck-they are not all up to date-have decided that this is the future for their community, that the gold mining economy cannot be bolstered up forever and that new industry is going to have to be provided for the people of that area with the assistance of the federal and provincial governments and a great deal of hard work on the part of the municipal officials all working toward this end.
This has been one of the problems we have faced. I am sure it is also true in the mari-times and in any area where there is an industry that is decaying and disappearing. This is particularly so in the case of mining, because the resource is not renewable. Yet you will find many municipal officials who are pledged to maintaining to the very end the economy of that industry. The situation is no different in the areas I represent or in any other area of Canada. We quite often find municipal officials pledged to maintaining something that is really disappearing and they are not looking forward to the day when something has to replace that which appears to be gone.
As I mentioned, there are assessable assets in any community. There are the people of the community who build their homes and raise their children there. The human asset is one of the most difficult to transfer from one place to another. We have all been aware of the difficulty that always arises with the displacement of labour within a given area, and trying to move that labour to another area where employment may be available. It is not only a question of the remaining that is necessary. There is the fact that people have their roots in the community, which I think gives a great deal of stability to any community and is a most valuable asset. Therefore I believe we should not think of moving people, but rather should think of making assets available that will make it possible for the community to flourish and be a success again.
4876	HOUSE OF
National Location of Industry Council
In each area there are community service assets such as streets, roads, hospitals and fire departments in addition to the new materials in the area. In any given area there is always some natural resource that is an asset to the development of industry in that area. While I am not suggesting that all industry should be based on natural resources, certainly the federal government can survey these assets if they provide this type of service to municipalities and provincial governments requesting it.
Lastly, one of the greatest assets any community can have is its transportation facilities. I am quite happy to say that in northern Ontario we have many forms of transportation which would be a vital asset to any industry wishing to settle in that area. So far as many commodities are concerned, there is no difference between moving them from areas close to Toronto or Hamilton and moving the same type of commodity from northern Ontario to Toronto. Coming north or going south there are none of the great traffic bottlenecks that there are in the metropolitan area, or in the Hamilton-Niagara area, from the point of view of the movement of transport trucks. I have been told by truck drivers that they can leave Kirkland Lake, unload in Toronto and be on their way within the same period of time as a transport coming from Hamilton to Toronto during the day. All it means is another eight or ten hours wages for the truck driver and another barrel or two of diesel oil. This is the main difference so far as transportation is concerned.
We also have the provincially owned railway which is willing to make concessions toward the development of industry, and this certainly will not be a roadblock in developing industry in northern Ontario. We also have air transportation, and as far as the people are concerned the transportation facilities generally are sufficient.
We have another asset that many people do not know about or have not paid any attention to, in that many of the gold mining communities are less than 200 miles from a salt water port. Rail facilities are available, and in time a large percentage of the flow of goods will be to Europe via the port of Moosonee.
In moving this resolution I do not expect that the government is going to accept it immediately because I think it takes a great deal of planning, a great deal of pushing and a lot of hollering before the federal government ever decides to move in any direction. I suggest that we will holler just as loud as the maritimers, but perhaps we will have to holler for a shorter period of time than they


did in getting assistance for their area, because I think the idea is generally accepted now that it is not a bad thing for the federal government to assist areas where such assistance is desired by the municipal and provincial governments.
I am sure that the areas of northern Ontario that I represent, particularly those dependent on the gold mining industry, have now come to the conclusion that they are going to have to have assistance from the federal government if they are going to be able to accomplish the secondary industrial development which they need. I should like to add in closing that in our areas community spirit is a very important factor. We do not want to displace our people. We want to use whatever method is possible to keep them there, and if the government wants to make a suggestion on the matter of relocation of industry I will be very happy to listen to any proposition they put forward and try to obtain the necessary support for it.
We have a unique situation in the gold mining industry. Eighty per cent of our people working in that industry are heads of families. Sixty per cent of them own their own homes. The average age of the people working in that industry is over 50 years. I think these factors will indicate to the house and to the country that there is a great desire on the part of these people to stay in that community and to find employment for the people we are training, because within a radius of 100 miles from Kirkland Lake we have the training facilities that will provide highly skilled and trained young people for any industrial development that can be brought to our area. At the present time these people are all being exported to southern Ontario, other parts of industrial Canada and to the United States. I believe that so far as our area is concerned retraining is not going to be the answer nor is relocation of the people. But if we investigate the possibilities that have been opened up by the developments in England and some of the northern European countries, we will be able to do something by way of relocating industry that will be much more satisfactory than relocating our citizens.

subtopic: INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL LOCATION COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of interest that I looked upon the motion put forward by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). As a matter of fact, a rather large part of the riding I have the honour to represent in this house is especially interested in industry. We already have firms that export quality products outside Quebec and are gaining an evergrowing reputation, which is saying a lot.

Indeed, who has not heard about the famous Belanger or L'Islet products, whether they be stoves, furnaces and refrigerators, or furniture, textiles and foodstuffs, to mention only those.
But it so happens that we also have a fairly great number of smaller industries which, unfortunately, are faced with too many thorny problems in the finance, labour, marketing and development fields.
It seems to me quite natural in this world of ours, in the middle of the twentieth century, that our areas should try desperately to get more industrialized, particularly in Quebec where we have to suffer an unforgivable lag compared to certain of the other provinces which, I have to admit it, managed to move ahead before we did. But let us not cry over spilt milk, let us face the future with more serenity, thanks to wiser measures which are better suited to our present and future needs.
However, I must say in passing that small industry, back home as elsewhere, is far from being sufficiently protected. It is being bled white and, on account of that, it is too often faced with impending bankruptcy because of our idleness, so we must act quickly. I wish to quote the famous words spoken by a former mayor of the city of Montreal, who was also a member of parliament: "Hurry up, it is urgent".
It is all very well to ask for the establishment of a national location council for industries in order to distribute them more evenly, but I agree with the hon. member for Timis-kaming when he says that we must also give adequate warranties of success at all levels, federal, provincial and municipal. Moreover, it is most urgent that before venturing too far in that field, we seek primarily to strengthen and improve the position of the small industries that already exist.
In my opinion, it is absolutely necessary to admit that loans must be made easier by revising credit restrictions and offering to those interested lower interest rates, to make it easier for them to meet their numerous obligations.
The services offered by the industrial financing bank in Quebec, for instance, fall far short of the demand; and when one wants a loan, the maximum amount is so low that it becomes more of a hindrance than a help.
With regard to the chartered banks, they have too often merged, with the result that our people are sent to Roy. Nat. or to what I would call other trusts of the same kind.
Even the income tax is endangering to an alarming extent the survival of small industries, when the advantages granted to bigger 28902-5-3114
National Location of Industry Council plants are considered. I feel it would be advisable to review our taxation system in that connection with the co-operation of the provinces.
That is why I add here that I strongly hope we will secure many tangible proofs of good will from our various governments in that respect, following the federal-provincial conference that will start right here in Ottawa in a few days.
Would we not find there, in that increased assistance to small industries, the ideal means to fight even more effectively unemployment which is the bane of our modern world? Personally, I am convinced of it, and I would dare say, in considering the countless number of small industries operating across our country -I am referring more particularly to the province of Quebec-that nearly 65 to 70 per cent of our unemployed would find jobs if such measures were adopted.
For instance, in wartime, if I am not mistaken, the government had implemented a policy under which it would pay a certain percentage, decreasing with the length of service, of the wages of newcomers or apprentices in some industrial trades. I am thinking for instance about printing or machine shops; we had thus placed on the labour market better qualified workers, men and women better prepared to make a place for themselves, a more desirable and more promising place which has kept improving ever since, as far as they are concerned.
Would it not be possible to consider similar measures, other than the one recently put into effect by the present government with regard to aged workers, and for which we commend it greatly?
We need not have any apprehensions about the participation of our municipalities in such a program, because there is already evidence that they are looking forward to such a measure; in this connection let me give you a concrete example taken in the municipality of Notre Dame Du Rosaire in my riding. Here are a few excerpts from the daily newspaper Le Soleil of Tuesday, October 29 last, in that regard:
In order to bolster the sagging economy of the small municipality of Notre Dame Du Rosaire, in the county of Montmagny, the local municipal councillors have just taken a step which is, so to speak, unique in the province.
As a matter of fact, the councillors of that municipality, which is presided over by the mayor, Mr. Joseph Morin, decided to grant a municipal tax exemption for a period of ten years to any industry which would settle in the municipality.
The municipality of Notre Dame Du Rosaire is situated on highway 26, a few miles from the county seat, Montmagny, and it has a population of 726.

National Location of Industry Council
To industries that would like to settle in Notre Dame Du Rosaire, that municipality offers excellent transportation facilities, namely highway 26 which is entirely paved, and the C.N.R. network. The municipality has waterworks and it is situated near the South river. Moreover, a lot of land is available at very reasonable prices for industrial purposes.
The economy of Notre Dame Du Rosaire being mostly based on logging and farming, it follows that the activity is on the down-grade.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, today:
The members of the municipal council show no preference as to the type of industry which could eventually settle there, as long as it can employ about 20 men all year round.
As you may realize it, that community is not that particular.
Here is, Mr. Speaker, an example likely to prompt us to proceed farther with our work.
Our most complete co-operation is assured to the government to which I have the honour to belong, but although I respect and favour the plan contemplated by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), I must at the same time, in all fairness and decency, point out that important achievement of the present administration, namely the establishment of a Department of Industry.
As was recently indicated by the minister in charge of that important department, there is no intention to take over the part of the provinces as regards the incentives to be provided for private industries.
Just recently, the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) stated:
That the objectives of his department were to set up close and continuous contacts with industrialists and businessmen, without overlooking any consultation with economic bodies already set up in the provinces.
He said that the federal government will only mind its own business, wishing to piay a part which it is often the only government in a position to play effectively because of its powers.
The minister then recalled that his department covered the whole range of industrial activities in Canada, from textiles to aeronautics, and he underlined that more emphasis would be put from now on, among other things, on the economic development of the communities most seriously affected by unemployment.
Spokesman for the Canadian manufacturing industry in the federal government, the Minister of Industry promised in no uncertain terms to fulfil that obligation and to seek the necessary co-operation of both the private industries and the provinces, in order to achieve a better solution to the economic problems of our country.

I would like to bring to the attention of my good friend from Timiskaming a booklet, courtesy of the Civil Service Commission of Canada, entitled, "Department of Industry,"

which outlines briefly but effectively the functions and the work of this new department. May I quote more specifically:
-the department will:
promote the establishment of industrial research and development facilitieswork in closest co-operation with provincial departments of industrywork with all agencies at various levels of federal, provincial and municipal government to provide industrial opportunities in designated areas.
The organization of the department follows as much as possible the natural groupings of industry. Within the 10 operational branches there are 33 divisions, each of which encompasses a major segment of an industrial group and centres its interest on an area of industry which is homogeneous as to raw materials, work processes and end-products.
The major role of the area development agency will be one of co-ordination and promotion. It will depend on line divisions and branches to do much of its research and program administration.
I think this gives an idea and proves to a certain extent I was right in mentioning the facts, as I have been doing so far.

Following the establishment of the department I have just mentioned, which has become an accomplished fact, and the statement of the minister concerned on the policy of the said department, I reached the conclusion that the motion of the hon. member for Timiskaming, commendable and well meaning though it may be, has practically no further object, since all he requests is now being happily realized by the present administration, which I want to congratulate, once more, for its successful venture in that important section of our economy I hope, nevertheless, the few remarks I have humbly and personally brought forward will be studied carefully, and, above all, will be implemented for the greatest good of my fellow citizens and of the country at large, for which, you may rest assured, they will be forever grateful.

subtopic: INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL LOCATION COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to discuss for a few minutes the motion of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). The areas to which it refers include the maritime provinces, and especially the constituency of Pictou which I represent. In that constituency the closing down of coal mines, which commenced about 13 years ago, has resulted in the causing of a labour surplus there. The men who worked in the coal mining industry were unable to get other work.
The largest employer in the area is the Eastern Car Company at Trenton, Nova Scotia, which manufactures rolling stock for the railways. The area is dependent a great deal on this type of industry. When engaged at full capacity it employs approximately

1,200 men, but the difficulty now is that the two main railways, the C.P.R. and the C.N.R., need only a certain number of cars and are going into specialization. This has made the area one of continuing labour surplus. It has been so designated by the government, and was also designated a labour surplus area by the former government.
What is needed is other types of secondary industry to employ the workmen in the area. Although the intentions of the hon. member are worthy of commendation, I am not quite sure I agree with his recommendation for a national location of industry council. We have many commissions and councils at present. We have the Atlantic development board; and when I questioned the Secretary of State, who is answerable to parliament for that board, I gathered from his remarks that the Atlantic development board was set up to look into matters of importance to the whole Atlantic area, to provide the necessary climate for development, to provide help in transportation and freight costs, and thereby help the whole area. I also understood that the area development agency under the new Department of Industry would be assisting in attracting new industries.
Perhaps as the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet (Mr. Berger) has just said, the terms of reference of the area development agency, under the Department of Industry, are wide enough to carry out the intentions expressed in the motion of the hon. member for Timiskaming, but I sincerely believe that extraordinary measures have to be taken to get areas, such as the one I represent, on their feet.
The hon. member for Timiskaming says that the council he seeks to establish would work in co-operation with the monetary and fiscal authorities to offer incentives in order to attract new industry. It can be pointed out that the former government introduced the incentive of double depreciation, and the present government, through the income tax bill passed recently, has given other forms of incentive. It can also be pointed out that the former government, through the then minister of finance, was able to attract an automobile plant to the Dartmouth area, the Volvo plant from Sweden. I am not an economist or a financier. I do not know what additional incentives would be needed, but in the present situation I feel something out of the ordinary has to be effected.
In the province of Nova Scotia a crown corporation, Industrial Estates Limited, has been set up. This has been able to attract a large number of small industries into the province, including the automobile plant. They construct buildings and rent them to firms, giving the firms an opportunity to
National Location of Industry Council purchase the buildings once they are on their feet. In a conversation with the president of that corporation, who lives in the same area as I do, I gathered he felt in order to assist areas such as ours there had to be additional help from the federal government. Industrial Estates have only so much in assets, and federal government assistance is necessary. As I have said, perhaps the new area development agency can carry out this role, but I believe it will have a lot of work to do, and I hope it will have the necessary machinery to do it.
In my own area there is a voluntary organization known as the Pictou county research and development commission. This was set up a few years ago and includes members of the clergy, the steel workers union and representatives of the industries in the county. This commission is attempting to do something for the area. I suggested at a meeting that they get in touch with the Atlantic development board. I believe they have done that, and they have also talked with Industrial Estates. I hope, once the area development agency is set up and the new Department of Industry starts to work, the agency will have people who can go there and talk to the members of this commission. This is a voluntary organization. It can do good work, and I think it is a most necessary thing.
I might point out that in that area the vocational school was opened this fall to help our younger people learn the necessary trades. A labour report was issued after the prime minister of the day, now the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), had representatives of the Department of Labour and the Department of Trade and Commerce go to the area and carry out a survey. The report was confidential at the time, but I have been able to see it. The report pointed out that the people in the area, even those who were older, could be educated in the various skills and trades, as well as the younger people. Therefore the necessary labour force is there.
As I said originally, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to speak very much longer on this matter. My own constituency is certainly the type that would be assisted by measures along the lines of the measure introduced by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). I repeat, they must be extraordinary measures in order to cure a chronic blight which the people of our area have suffered. A couple of good sized industries brought into the area would make all the difference in the world and would give the people of Pictou county a glimmer of light. About two years ago the former government arranged, by way of export credits to assist the Dominion Steel and

It was estimated that the order, amounting to about $25 million, would keep that plant running for approximately a year. Unfortunately a revolution occurred and the order was of course cancelled. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read this evening the notice of motion of the hon. member for Timiska-ming (Mr. Peters); incidentally, the hon. member's constituency is close to mine, in the northwest section of Ontario. It seems to me that the notice of motion rests upon serious motives. Its objectives are similar to those embodied in legislation brought in by the government not so long ago.
Here is the hon. member's notice of motion:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the establishment of a national location of industry council for the purpose of directing new industries into those regions of the country which are dependent on a narrow industrial base...
I am thinking, at the moment, of some regions where that base is very narrow indeed. Take for instance our own area: La Peine, Rouyn, Noranda, Val d'Or, Malartic, Cadillac, Amos. It goes without saying that it would be a good thing if new industries were implanted there. A moment ago, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Berger) spoke to us of the needs of his constituency for new industries.
However, Mr. Speaker, in spite of the fact that all these objectives are highly commendable, and that the motives are very weighty, it must be admitted that the results obtained so far are not very satisfactory, good intentions notwithstanding. Our section of the country is marking time; no new industries have sprouted there, and we seem content to listen to the goodwill statements of the government and of certain members of our assembly.
This morning, before I left Rouyn, I inquired about the number of unemployed in our area. In November 1963, there are over 1,600 unemployed. Family heads are clamouring for jobs: we suggested they try the winter works program and some found jobs there.

This morning, I had the visit of two bachelors, two young Canadians who want to earn a living. One of them was over 40 and the other one was only 23. The U.I.C. office in Rouyn told them: "You are bachelors and we have to give priority to heads of families." We understand that a father who has many children to support certainly needs more assistance than a bachelor.
However, what are we going to do about bachelors under this well-meaning system?

speechtext:
I hear my hon. friend from Cochrane say that they only have to get married. They cannot even afford to do so.
Mr. Speaker, it is easy to say to Canadian bachelors:	"Get married", but where are
they going to find the money to do so? Where will they find the job that will make it possible for them to consider matrimony?
Those are not solutions, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) meant well when he introduced this motion because we do need new industries but we have been talking of new industries in northwestern Quebec and northeastern Ontario for ten years now.
The government is well intentioned. It encourages industries to establish themselves in the so-called depressed areas. In spite of those good intentions, just go and see whether a single new industry has settled in those areas following the legislation which was introduced recently by the present government and which grants a tax holiday to new industries which would settle in depressed areas.
Mr. Speaker, the notice of motion of the hon. member for Timiskaming goes on as follows:
-and empowering the national location of industry council, in co-operation with the monetary and fiscal authorities, to offer incentives to attract new industry to such regions when requested by provincial and municipal governments.
Now, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet was right when he said a few moments ago that the government had already enacted legislation to that end.
-to offer incentives to attract new industry-
However, we are still at the same point. We are grappling with the problem in Bill No. C-105 since it intends to create new jobs or to help retrain workers displaced or replaced by machines, enabling them to get some training, to become technicians, to acquire new skills in order to be in a position finally to find work.
Now, once again in spite of all those fine intentions, under the present system, an unemployed worker is trained, and instead of having an unskilled unemployed worker,

you have a trained one, who will still be without work. Moreover, there are many such workers in our firms and industries. For example, in my own business in Rouyn, I keep two or three employees-why? So that they will earn a livelihood during winter- while I could have done without their services very easily during that season. Now, these employees have remained in my service so that they could provide for their family and children. I believe our employers do likewise, in order to prevent many Canadian families from being poverty stricken.
Mr. Speaker, I endorse this motion whose purpose is to direct new industries towards our regions and our depressed areas, to develop Canada's natural resources and to help heads of families and our youth improve their lot. If we could do that, I believe we would have achieved something worth-while but I doubt very much that it will be so because automation is making constant inroads with the result that it is difficult for men to earn their living.
We, on this side of the house, are quite willing to co-operate and to go along with the experiments that are suggested but let us do something, let us encourage the establishment of new industries and let us see what will happen in five or ten years from now. That is fine but I hope it will be possible for me, at some other time, to express my views and to set forth a constructive program for the development of Canada's tremendous resources and possibilities. Then, I think Social Credit will have made its contribution to our legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak briefly on this measure, for I believe there is much in it to commend itself to the attention of the house. In my constituency recently a seminar was held at Bridgewater to discuss the recurrent problem of winter unemployment. This seminar was attended by municipal councillors, wardens of the municipality and mayors of the different towns in the area, and their problem in that section of Lunenburg county was the traditional one of unemployment during the winter period. We know that this is a seasonal situation; but we have industrious, ambitious people in that section of Lunenburg county, and I believe part of their problem could be solved if secondary industry could be induced to locate in that area. It is quite possible that with the extra incentives suggested in this motion of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) new industries would locate there.
The idea proposed by the hon. member is not new. I recently returned from the United
National Location of Industry Council Kingdom where I had the opportunity of sitting in the British house of commons and listening to proposals put forward. These were recorded in the Daily Mail and I believe are worthy of mention:
Top priority is to be given to the socially depressed northeast in the government's plans for modernizing Britain.
Its population of 2,875,000 will get a bigger share than any other part of the country of expenditure on new roads, houses, schools and factories.
There is to be a continuous improvement in all public services, from libraries and swimming baths to street lighting and parks.
These and other great changes are envisaged as part of the biggest recovery operation for an area hit by high unemployment ever conceived and sanctioned by a British government.
The program for the northeast and another for Scotland, published yesterday as white papers, call for long term investment costing scores of millions of pounds.
I believe something of this nature should be done. When the Conservative party were in power we made a start along these lines. Our subsidies for shipbuilding were a great inducement toward providing employment, especially in Nova Scotia, where our shipyards are booming. But while this has provided employment for a section of our people, there are still some citizens who throughout the winter period are unemployed. I feel that something outstanding must lie done. I do not agree that a national location of industry council should be set up. We already have a new Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) and I believe these areas are now known to the minister and his assistants. I think it would be possible to consult with those provincial and municipal authorities who are well aware of the problem and who could give valuable information to the new department as to what industries could be located in these depressed areas, areas where there is unemployment, and new measures thereby brought into effect which would assist new industry to locate there. I think extraordinary measures are needed. For too long were we in Nova Scotia looked upon as the depressed mari-times. In my view, now that we have the Atlantic development board, this is one problem which could be referred to it, and in consultations between the directors of that board and the new Department of Industry I believe new incentives would bring about an improved situation which would help the areas most affected by unemployment, especially in Nova Scotia.

subtopic: TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING ASSISTANCE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned at five o'clock, I was saying that the house should give a lot of attention to the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act because of its great influence on the career of a great number of Canadians.
The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) had been concerned for a long time with the question of technical and vocational training. Therefore, as soon as he was appointed minister of labour, he called for a detailed study of the matter. He did not want to enter lightly into such a complex field. And before launching such a program, he wanted first to know the means then at the government's disposal in order to avoid useless duplication.
The provinces were then invited to make their needs known so that a general program that could give satisfaction to all interested parties could be formulated.
These studies have led to the conclusion that the total cost of construction works required to get the program under way was approximately $511 million. Out of that amount, the federal contribution totalled $326 million.
Last week, the hon. member for Ontario told us that the capital mentioned resulted in the construction of 254 new schools, 4 institutes of technology and 47 trade schools.
These new facilities make it possible to accommodate 138,000 new students each year. Fast developments in education, in every aspect, require constant efforts to keep up to date in the field of education as well as the field of vocational training.
I am pleased that the authorities of my province decided to avail themselves of the advantages offered by this legislation initiated by the previous Conservative government.
I have in my hand a summary indicating the projects approved in the province of Quebec between April 1, 1961, and March 14, 1962. It is indicated that 19 institutions in our province benefited from the provisions of this legislation. The estimated construction costs of those institutions was close to $11.25 million with a federal participation of nearly $8 million. The said institutions can provide facilities for some 2,550 students.
It is with pleasure that I bring to the attention of the house the fact that two institutions in the city of St. Hyacinthe took advantage of this act, a Conservative conception. It was, first of all, the textile institute which received grants totalling close to $36,000 for the purchase of machinery and equipment. Then, a

grant of $3 million was paid out for the purpose of helping in the construction of the farm technology institute and the buildings are under construction.
Besides the substantial grants just mentioned, several industrial training classes were organized by the local unemployment insurance office for the unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the importance of the textile industry in the province of Quebec, and more particularly in the constituency I have the honour to represent in this house, I plan to direct the rest of my remarks to the need of preparing the technicians and leaders needed in that important sector of our economy.
The primary textile industry is the second largest employer in the province. It provides work to approximately 44,000 workers and the gross value of its production reaches more than $500 million every year. There are primary textile factories in a hundred localities of the province of Quebec. It is essential, therefore, to provide for the technical training of the personnel required to take charge of this industry which is so important for our workers.
According to a recent survey, 3,000 more workers having received a technical training will be required in the textile industry of Quebec within the next ten years.
The same survey has shown that in 1960, 2,500 persons were employed in administrative and technical positions. Moreover, it has been estimated that as a result of separation due to illness or retirement, the textile industry in Quebec needs at the present time at least 75 new graduates in textile each year.
In 1970, at least 150 graduates will be required each year to meet the needs of this typical Quebec industry.
According to the experts' estimates and provided that the domestic market and imports follow their present trends, the Canadian textile industry will provide jobs for 121,000 workers in 1970.
I, therefore, urge the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) to devote his full attention to this problem, reminding him that the St. Hyacinthe textile institute is administered by a qualified staff who has already trained a large number of technicians and professionals in the textile industry. In fact, those professionals and technicians now hold prominent positions in industry not only in Quebec but throughout Canada.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska (Mr. Pepin) will undoubtedly agree with me that the director of the St. Hyacinthe textile institute and his loyal associates will co-operate extensively with the proper authorities to ensure the continuation of this
Vocational Training Assistance Act project in the province of Quebec which came to life under another government and which received subsidies from the previous Conservative government, to train leaders who will be able to make a success out of the Quebec textile industry in the interests of the province and of the country at large.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words with regard to the bill now before us, and particularly as to the amendments having to do with the provision of training to persons in industry. I should like to ask the minister if the legislation is going to help apprenticeship training in industry. I do not feel that the act covers apprenticeship training and I should like to speak on this point for a few minutes. First may I say that our country must feel embarrassed at times at having to go abroad to secure skilled workers for our industries when there are so many unemployed people throughout the country.
Apprenticeship schemes existing in a variety of industries are subject to the uncertainties of Canada's economy. Many schemes do not have legal recognition, as a result of which the government insists that, come depression or boom, apprentices will be guaranteed their full term of training. However, apprentices in a few designated trades are protected in Ontario by a government training program. Outside these designated trades management, conscientious as it may or may not be, has no obligation to apprentices. If lay-offs are necessary the apprentice may be asked to leave in the middle of his training.
There is no general scheme whereby this half-trained young man can be absorbed by his industry elsewhere in Canada so that his training will not be interrupted. He is left to his own resources. He may have to seek entirely different work and he is always susceptible to the temptation of higher wages in a job having a limited future. An unscrupulous employer can also take an apprentice on with the sole purpose of gaining cheap labour. When depression hits the plant a fully trained journeyman, unless protected by a union contract, can be laid off and the apprentice kept on to take over at a lower wage.
This shortsightedness on the part of the employer has raised the ire and the suspicions of labour. The result is that most unions insist on rigid seniority clauses in their contracts to protect the journeymen. A certain number of apprentices are permitted in ratio to journeymen and, if necessary, lay-offs abide by the same ratio. Out of all this situation arguments come from both sides. Management accuses labour of sacrificing apprentices in times of lay-off. Labour accuses management of using apprentices for selfish

Vocational Training Assistance Act ends when they should be treating them as an operational cost and an investment in the future of their particular industry.
This situation is not general. Many companies have apprenticeship plans that are working to the satisfaction of management and labour. The Ontario government has made some advancement in implementing training programs, and each province has been assisted by the federal act which was brought forward by the former Conservative government. I should like to quote two gentlemen, one a union leader and the other a factory manager, in order to point out their views in regard to apprenticeship training. Mr. Ralph Sullivan of the united electrical union has this to say:
Companies tend to render the subject of apprenticeship to the rise and fall of production. We are naturally opposed to the journeyman being laid off so that management can eventually bring in new, untrained people as cheap labour. Management must take on the obligation of training new workers but not at the expense of experienced men with established service.
Lack of Incentive among young men toward apprenticeship is not governed by high wages in other occupations. It is simply because industry will not guarantee them being able to serve their full time. No security is offered. This is what is discouraging youngsters. I know examples where a man has had to spend eight years of his life instead of four to get his trade because his training has been deferred by lay-offs.
Mr. Robert Barrett, factory manager, has this to say:
An apprentice must be guaranteed his training time. Perhaps the best idea would be to have a training scheme that is outside of labour's seniority clauses and beyond the reach of management as a source of cheap labour. Management-labour committees could be set up within industries to protect apprentices along these lines.
Government should have a hand in this, of course, perhaps on a provincial basis but within a national scheme so that an apprentice can go elsewhere if he is affected by lay-offs. The provincial government-
Mr. Barrett is speaking of the Ontario government.
-has already done a lot of groundwork on this problem but could be more directly involved. Perhaps governments could subsidize apprentices by paying part of their wages while they are training on the job. This would take some of the onus off management and assure labour that the apprentices are protected.
One can see from these two quotations that these men, leaders in their own fields, are interested in apprenticeship training. There is a lot of talk about the need for expansion in industry, but how can we expand if we have not got the skilled labour? I feel that the Department of Labour, and especially the minister, should give serious thought to instigating proper legislation to improve our apprenticeship training program. It should be possible to secure men for skilled trades in Canada. We
should not have to go outside the country to find the necessary skilled workers.

subtopic: TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING ASSISTANCE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we are considering this question of further assistance to the vocational and technical training of the young people of the country I look upon it as a very happy coincidence that parliament at the present time is considering the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, because these two matters can be intermeshed to the benefit of Canada and Canadian taxpayers as a whole. When the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare were introduced on Thursday the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Cassel-man) and the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Slogan) pointed out that, with such vast expenditures being made by this second greatest spending department of the government, there must be opportunities for reducing expenditures if they are closely examined month by month and year by year.
Speaking along the same theme on Thursday night, I made the suggestion that the first big cut that could be made in the expenditures of the Department of National Health and Welfare, one which would save many of the provincial prepaid hospital insurance schemes now in jeopardy, would be to transfer the training of student nurses from the departments of health in the ten provinces to the departments of education. I pointed out at that time the departments of education of the ten provinces now train young people for every career, trade and vocation there is, except nursing. I suggested that by putting nursing under the departments of education, money would be saved the departments of health.
The Ontario government is making haste slowly in this direction. I sincerely want to compliment them and commend them for what they are doing under the direction of the Hon. Dr. Dymond, the minister of health, and the Hon. William Davis, minister of education. The Ontario government, under the department of education, has been conducting for some years a course for registered nursing assistants at the Beal technical school in London, Ontario, where they are graduating registered nursing assistants. About four years ago they extended this effort to a school in my own riding of York-Humber, the Weston collegiate and vocational institute which now has a course for registered nursing assistants.
I point out that these courses in the Beal technical school in London, Ontario and the Weston collegiate and vocational institute in Weston are under the department of education. This has been a great departure on the

part of the provincial department of health in putting these courses under the department of education. In addition, the province of Ontario, with the ready co-operation of the Hon. Dr. Dymond and under the careful eye of the Hon. William Davis, is instituting a new course for nurses at the Ryerson polytechnical institute. The legislation now before us lends itself to adaptation for the education of nurses throughout the ten provinces.
It is the great anomaly of the present day that, when we have so many unemployed throughout the country, the one vocation that could use more and more employees is nursing and other hospital employment. There is nothing but a shortage of applicants in this area. This is due primarily, of course, to the lack of pay the graduate nurse can expect to receive upon graduation. Second, it is due to the present method of education of nurses. Many young girls resent the convent-like atmosphere of being in by ten every night of the week with one late night in the month. They would sooner have freedom and train for secretaries, stenographers, artists or any other vocation but nursing, because under the nursing education system in use they are cabined and confined in their student days.
By moving the education of nurses over to the department of education under the legislation we are now considering, great assistance can be given to the provincial governments for the education of persons to become registered nurses. It is true that student nurses for generations past, and at the present time, are largely confined to that class between 18 and 22 years of age. I would urge upon the ten provincial governments to give serious consideration to training, under the moneys made available to them under this legislation, married women between the ages of 35 and 40. It seems that in this day and generation women give up bearing children by the age of 30. By the time they are 35 or 36, the youngest child is in school and the mother is at home alone during the day. If attention were paid to educating married women from 35 to 40 and they were advised that they would be trained as registered nurses or certified nursing assistants at a nearby collegiate, vocational or technical school, I am certain that thousands of women would be attracted to this new avenue of employment.
I would suggest that the students who go to these technical and vocational schools, with the assistance provided by this legislation, should be paid by the hour for the work they do at the hospitals where they will be given their clinical experience. Their lectures could be taken in vocational and technical schools or at university buildings, if close; but the clinical experience would be gained at the
Vocational Training Assistance Act hospital, where they would be paid at the going rate for the work they do. With these women, both the girls from 18 to 22 with whom we are familiar and the proposed new class of possible nurses, the married women from 35 to 40, I am certain we would attract a large number of applicants, because they would be paid for the work they are doing and thus be able to look after their own expenses while in training.
Of course, suggestions such as these, and the actions of the Ontario department of education in assuming the education of certain nursing assistants in London, in Weston and at the Ryerson polytechnical institute in Toronto, are meeting with a great deal of cluck-clucking on the part of the women who for years have dominated nursing education in hospitals. They are always "viewing with alarm." The provinces have to take a deep interest in this field of nursing education now and for the next few years, because it is the dominant fact facing hospital administrators today.
In the Ottawa Citizen of Friday, November 8, there is an editorial entitled, "The Need for More Nurses". This editorial comments on a motion passed at the 1963 convention of the Ontario hospitals association in which that association urged the provincial government to assume the major responsibility for providing new facilities for training nurses. The motion points out that the efforts of hospitals, universities and the nursing profession have failed to meet the existing demand for nurses. The Ottawa Citizen states that when the Ontario hospital services commission was brought into effect, the Ontario government had the obligation of seeing that there are enough nurses to support the scheme. The Citizen is commenting on the motion of the Ontario hospitals association, but the statement that it is incumbent upon the provincial government to see that there are enough nurses to staff the prepaid hospital scheme applies equally to all the ten provinces as it does to the province of Ontario.
The Toronto Globe and Mail, under date of October 15, commented editorially on a report presented to the provincial government by a committee of experts representing the nursing and medical profession, the nursing schools, hospitals and the Ontario hospitals services commission. This report advised the Ontario government to institute a crash program of training in order to get sufficient nurses to staff the hospitals now in existence, and those about to be built. This report states that instead of graduating 2,500 nurses a year as at present, it will be necessary by 1968 for Ontario to graduate 5,000. With graduate nurses from 18 to 22, experience shows that

Vocational Training Assistance Act within four years 75 per cent of the girls are married and only 25 per cent of them are left at work.
If the provincial governments will take advantage of the legislation now being passed -I am certain it will be passed because the Conservatives state that they fathered the bill and the Liberal party is like a mother hen clucking over it-I am sure we will have a very good hatch. I am sure if provincial governments will take advantage of the assistance available to them to put nurses in training in existing buildings, they will be able to produce the number of nurses recognized as necessary, if the hospitals are to operate at their maximum capacity.
The Globe and Mail refers to a crash program for nurses, and this is as good a description as any that can be applied to the present necessity. Some years ago there was a tremendous shortage of school teachers, particularly in the secondary schools, and then in the primary schools. The provinces instituted crash programs whereby they gave certificates of teaching ability, to students who had just finished grade 12, for public school teaching, and to students who had just finished university for secondary school teaching. With the crash programs, in a matter of about four years there was a plethora of graduate teachers, and we found that with the shortage of teachers salaries had moved up, so much so that educated persons who were qualified teachers were leaving business to return to the profession.
If teachers will leave business to return to the teaching profession, as has been proven in the case of schools, through the lure of higher pay, then it can be done with regard to the shortage of nurses. There are thousands and thousands of graduate nurses now married; and with a premium rate of pay for holiday and Sunday work, and shift differentials, they can be attracted back from their homes into the gaps that exist in our nursing field. But it is necessary that even more younger and inexperienced people be trained in this field at this time. I sincerely hope that the departments of education will realize that this is, shall I say, a parliamentary-sent opportunity, to introduce the training of nurses under departments of education, with assistance from the federal Department of Labour.
Of course we are going to hear loud out-crys from defenders of the status quo: Where will the teachers come from? I can only suggest on this occasion that during crash programs the teachers for graduate nurses or certified nursing assistants should be routed throughout the provinces in much the same way as are the assize court judges. They travel from county to county holding courts, and 

because of their legal training, ability and experience they are highly respected in the county court towns where they preside. If teachers now holding forth in schools of nursing should be circulated among new schools of nursing, under the heading of technical and vocational training assistance, they would bring the same high experience to the students.
About three years ago a leader in the field of nursing commented to me that the way nurses are being educated in hospitals leaves much to be desired in some fields, and pointed out there can be a town X where the instructress in maternity will pass all the student nurses of her school on provincial examinations, and the instructress in medicine, not being of high calibre, will have a great number of failures; but in town Y you will find a very expert teacher of student medicine will pass all her nurses, whereas the teacher in maternity, not being of the same high calibre, will have half her students fail. By having experienced teachers travel from school to school a greater majority of the students will pass.
I have already suggested, when speaking on the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, that we should drop the federal grants for nursing education. This will result not only in the expenses under that heading being transferred to another, namely education, but it will at least be in its proper perspective. If departments of education can train doctors and dentists, they certainly can train nurses.
There is an article in this morning's Globe and Mail which points out that, because of growing specialization in medical practice, many patients are losing their identification once they enter hospital doors. So many experts look at a patient today that the doctor does not know the patient and the patient does not know the doctor. The article is illustrated with an interesting cartoon in which a patient is lying in bed, and is looking up and saying, "I realize it is none of my business, doctor, but how am I doing"?
This can be adapted to the taxpayers of the country. The country is being besieged at all hours of the day and night by minions of the nursing hierarchy throughout Canada who are urging, "No change, no change, no change." The Globe and Mail says we have to have a change; we must have the crash education programs; so that we can turn out 5,000 nurses a year instead of the present 2,500 in Ontario. I presume the figures are relative for the rest of Canada, but we must have an increase in salaries in order to attract girls into this profession. The incentives held out through the legislation we are now discussing will help attain that end, and I would

point out to the 10 departments of education in the country that the federal government is willing to consider adapting these grants to nursing education under the heading of technical and vocational guidance.
I had not intended to make any reference to the comments of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) and the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Weichel), in which they were claiming great credit for having introduced this idea of technical and vocational training assistance. If they were getting satisfaction out of the claim it is quite satisfactory with me; but when the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) stood up this afternoon and stated he well remembered the day in 1960 when the former administration had brought in this great assistance to technical and vocational guidance, I became a little provoked. Surely he remembers that great Canadian, C. D. Howe, who as long ago as 1942 introduced technical and vocational assistance to the schools of the provinces of Canada, in order to get aircraftsmen and air technical crews to make the R.C.A.F. the finest fighting air force in the world.
We have no objection to those who fanned into flame in 1960 the embers of the vocational assistance act of C. D. Howe which operated from 1942 to 1947. I know whereof I speak, because after the war I was able to secure a grant, with the co-operation of the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Cameron) who was then in the house, of $700,000 to help build the George Harvey vocational school in the riding of York South. That was the last grant made under the vocational assistance wartime act; and that was in 1947. There is no finer technical school in the province than the George Harvey vocational school, and it was made possible, I would advise the hon. member for Port Arthur, by the genuine and generous co-operation of the then hon. member for Port Arthur.

The objective of an industrial system.
In attacking an engineering problem the first point we settle, with as much exactness as possible, is our objective. Under those circumstances, what could we do to find jobs for everyone?

Let us take, for instance, the case of an automated modern plant employing 500 men whose average yearly salary is $4,000. This means a total of $2 million distributed as salaries every year by an automated industry.
On the other hand, let us take another plant, which has not been modernized and which employs 1,000 men (instead of 500) and who receive also $4,000 a year. The operating costs of this plant would amount to $4 million instead of $2 million.
By cutting the work week in half, in order that both plants may attain equal production the following result would follow. In the plant employing 1,000 men instead of 500, reducing by half the working hours would cost $4 million a year.
Now, in the second plant which is not automated and not modernized, and which employs 2,000 men instead of 1,000 expenditures for salaries would amount to $8 million a year. The inevitable result would be that the non-automated plant would have to close shop and yield its place to another plant more modern and better adjusted to new conditions.

I have here a volume of the report submitted by the royal commission on constitutional problems. A few years ago, an inquiry was held which gave all the Quebec organizations an opportunity to express their views and their wishes. Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to pages 288 and 289 of volume 2, book 3, of 1956:
The province of Quebec and the federal grants
This scrupulous adherence to the principle of federalism has been clearly obvious and has imposed heavy sacrifices in the field of taxation, especially as regards the question of grants, which is the main issue in the controversy between the federal government and the provinces.
Like the other provinces, the province of Quebec accepts the statutory grants provided for in the constitution. It even went as far as to ask, in 1887 and in 1907, that they be reviewed. Those grants were established to compensate for taxes which the provinces were compelled to surrender: without such a surrender, confederation would not have been possible. It should not be wondered therefore that the provinces seek from time to time to have this compensation adjusted according to the rights yielded, as their extent is being revealed. There is nothing in this contrary to the confederation act of 1867.
The same does not apply to conditional and fiscal grants which the federal government has made, especially in the last 20 years, one of the instruments of its constitutional policy. Fiscal grants are paid by way of compensation for taxes the surrender of which by the provinces is in no way essential to the stability of the state. In fact, it is the very opposite that is true: as long as the federal system is not abolished, the proper operation of the state requires that the provinces keep taxation powers proportionate to the extent of their constitutional obligations. The province of Quebec preferred to do without substantial revenues rather than agree to a system of grants involving a lessening of its autonomy and a surrender of its prerogatives.
Listen closely to this, Mr. Speaker:
If the province agreed at times to the payment of conditional grants, as in the case of technical training and old age pensions (1st stage), it is due to the false position in which the interference of the federal government in fields outside of its jurisdiction unavoidably place the provinces.
By refusing federal grants as it did in various circumstances, the province of Quebec not only deprives itself of amounts that are being made available to it but contributes, through federal taxes, to the amounts taken advantage of by the other provinces which are less concerned about federalist loyalty.
In short, and this is the major point to remember in these history pages, in taxation as in all other

constitutional matters, Quebec's stand has never changed: it abides by the interpretation according to the spirit of federalism of the agreement concluded in 1867.

That is why I am asking the federal government and the provinces at the next federal-provincial conference to find the necessary means to provide a final solution.

Mr. Speaker, there are times when it is really interesting to take part in debates and today's discussion seems doubly interesting, because it proves once more that everyone agrees on the seriousness of the unemployment problem.
Here, I should like to refer to an address delivered by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Vocational Training Assistance Act MacEachen) in this house on June 10. I think we all agree with what he said. I quote:
The government is convinced that we cannot continue to tolerate the excessively high levels of unemployment of recent years. Over the past five years, unemployment has averaged 6.6 per cent of the labour force.
And he went on:
The stimulation of employment and the reduction of unemployment are major problems which the government is determined to tackle vigorously.
We must recognize, Mr. Speaker, that in the last few weeks, the government has launched a very unusual effort to find a solution to that especially thorny matter.
And the minister went on:
It is now widely recognized that the growth of our economy and the stimulation of employment are greatly facilitated by the improvement of the quality and skills of youth entering the labour force and by the adaptation of workers to constantly changing job requirements. The need for adaptation and retraining of our labour force is a consequence of a much stepped up rate of technological change in recent years.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-105, dealing with training of workers, technical and vocational training, should prompt us to give more consideration to the unemployment problem.
Of course, like everybody else, we realize we are faced with a problem due to a large degree to automation which is constantly spreading and takes jobs away from our workers. Consequently, that is one of the causes of unemployment.
There are also the demands of industry for a more skilled and more specialized labour.
I think that the bill which is really aimed at the training of that manpower, comes at an opportune time and will allow people who are affected by almost chronic unemployment to train for new jobs which will meet the needs of industry.
Past results were good in nine Canadian provinces; I make one exception: the province of Quebec. Great numbers of workers were trained and given new jobs, thanks to the training received in special training schools. Everywhere in Canada schools were erected and they have certainly become an asset for those provinces.
The fact is that a delicate problem remains, that of the province of Quebec. I shall not labour the point further because other speakers have talked about it eloquently enough so as to make the Minister of Labour and members of the cabinet realize that our situation is not similar to that of the other provinces, that we are a separate province. And, as the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) pointed out so well, the fact remains that Quebec, on
4894	HOUSE OF
Vocational Training Assistance Act account of the terms of the legislation, did not enjoy fully its benefits. Special arrangements ought to be taken so that Quebec workers may enjoy the benefits of the legislation.
I readily understand, Mr. Speaker, that it is difficult, at a given moment, to legislate in order to meet the needs of Canadians from coast to coast, the needs of a country made up of two different nations. But I think that we should not forget the fact that we have rights and privileges, and that we want to keep them.
Mr. Speaker, I would like also to take advantage of these few minutes to make suggestions to the Minister of Labour with regard to the training of technical labour. In my opinion, the Minister of Labour would benefit greatly from further consultation with the labour organizations of the country in order to receive from them appropriate suggestions with regard to labour problems and, in particular that which we are dealing with at this time, that is, technical and vocational training.
It seems that there is an increasing tendency towards centralization, in short greater importance is given to the central government. But I think that if this government really wants to assume its responsibilities and attain its objectives it must necessarily call upon these in-between bodies that are labour organizations and movements.
Mr. Speaker, it is an undeniable fact that we must gather up all our energies in order to find a solution to the unemployment problem. Workers' training, of course, is one of the solutions-but not the only one-which is before us tonight. In my opinion, the special committee established by the Senate, to inquire into the matter of manpower and employment, prompts us precisely to work in that direction. If I may, I shall quote one of the findings of that committee. Here it is:
Unskilled labour made up a greater proportion of the total monthly registration in metropolitan districts and large industrial areas with a labour surplus, than in the two other kinds of surplus areas in the labour market.
Obviously, the members of that committee found that in the communities where workers are unskilled, unemployment is higher and more acute. We should therefore pool all our resources to train qualified labour, which will not only answer the needs of industry to the greater benefit of industrial enterprise, but will also be of advantage to the working class and, consequently, the whole Canadian people.

In beginning my brief remarks at this stage of the proceedings on this bill, I wish to thank all hon. members for their contributions to this debate. I want to say a special word of thanks to my fellow Nova Scotian, the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates), for his kind remarks as he began his speech this afternoon.
The debate has ranged over a very wide field, in so far as any of the suggestions that have been made relate to technical and vocational training, they will be given the fullest possible consideration by the Department of Labour. As hon. members will realize, the general framework for the national system of technical and vocational training is set forth in the act respecting technical and vocational training assistance. The act as a whole is not before us. We have before us an amending bill, confined to a number of specific items in the act itself. There are five of these items.
One amendment increases the federal contribution of living allowances paid by a province to unemployed persons receiving training, from 75 per cent to 90 per cent. This increases that portion of the federal contribution for this phase of the training program to 90 per cent, or an increase of 15 per cent.
In addition to that we propose by another amendment to increase the contribution made by the federal government to costs incurred by provinces in training programs in industry, from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. Hon. members will appreciate that relatively little progress has been made in this important field of training in industry. For that reason we expect to give this phase of technical and vocational training a greater impetus by increasing the percentage assistance from 50 per cent to 75 per cent.
It might be of interest to hon. members to know that this particular phase of the program will extend to training programs in industry covering apprenticeship training, the problem which engaged the attention of the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Stenson). This will apply to basic educational development, to programs in industry providing basic education to employees, to place them in a position to acquire skill in advanced jobs or advanced technology.
The third phase of this training program in industry is to provide assistance for training to meet prospective automation. Even though the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Ca-ouette) dealt with automation in his speech, he did not relate his comments to this provision of the amending bill, which will allow employers to collaborate with the provinces, with federal assistance, to accelerate training in industry for employees whose skills may

become obsolete as a result of automation and who, if there is a response to this program, can be placed in a position to acquire additional skills.
The third aspect of the amending bill is to extend the time period for the additional 25 per cent for the provision of capital facilities for technical and vocatonal training. There is no doubt that a great expansion in training facilities has taken place under this program. On Tuesday of last week I assisted at the opening of a new college of trades and technology at St. John's, Newfoundland, a splendid institution that will have a great impact on the economy of that province. I want to tell the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) that on that occasion the premier of Newfoundland expressed publicly his appreciation of the work and co-operation he had received from the hon. member for Ontario during his period as minister of labour.
