As I say, the premier took that opportunity to express the appreciation of the government of Newfoundland to the hon. member for Ontario, whose efforts in this field have not gone unrecognized, at least in that province of Canada.
The purpose of this particular amendment, as hon. members will know, is to permit all provinces of Canada to participate to the maximum achieved up until March 31 of this year by the province of Newfoundland. The per capita contribution of the federal government in the age group 15 to 19 years reached $480 for the province of Newfoundland. This amendment will allow all provinces to achieve that maximum up until the expiry of the agreement in 1967.
For example, it will permit the province of Quebec, whose per capita quota is $51, to participate to the extent of $480 per capita in that age group. This amendment is of particular importance to the province of Quebec where many additional millions of dollars will be made available for the expansion of training facilities. The same is true to a lesser extent for all other provinces, except the province of Newfoundland.
The additional two amendments are to increase the numbers on the advisory council to permit greater participation by employer and union groups, and finally to provide an honorarium for the chairman.
The increased rate of assistance for training, especially training the unemployed, and for training programs in industry, underlines the urgent priority the government attaches to these aspects of the Canadian system of technical and vocational training. We cer-
Vocational Training Assistance Act tainly support the priority of these aspects of the program which was attached to them by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), who was concerned that our training program ought to be directed towards providing skills and training for jobs.
In his speech the hon. member for Port Arthur-and I may say his speech was very interesting to me-regarded the emphasis placed on the expansion of secondary school facilities as at the expense, in his view, of technical and trades schools. It may be that varying emphasis has been placed on secondary schools in particular provinces, but in general the approach has been balanced, and there has been a balanced program of expansion in secondary schools and in technical and trade schools.
It ought to be pointed out, of course, that the federal government participates in the secondary school program in order to support exclusively technical and vocational education and that aspect of the secondary school program which the federal government supports, namely technical and vocational education, enables students to enter the labour market more easily, and later to take more specialized training for employment. So, it is very wrong to suggest that an emphasis on secondary and vocational training is not job directed. It most certainly is.
I realize that this problem of technical and vocational training is a complex one. It might have been possible to have a general debate on the subject if the amending bill provided the opportunity. However, it does not. All I want to say in conclusion is that the national system of technical and vocational training is set out in the principal measure, the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act. It enables the federal government to enter into agreements with provincial governments to make substantial contributions to all aspects of technical and vocational training. There are ten aspects of technical and vocational training for which authority exists for the Minister of Labour to enter into agreements with the provinces. The emphasis given by any province to any particular program for which assistance is available is entirely up to the province itself. If any particular province has placed an emphasis on technical and vocational training at the secondary school level, that is a result of a decision by that province exercising its constitutional responsibility in that field.
The federal government has attempted to indicate its own estimate of priorities by the particular range and rates of contributions it has assigned under these various programs. Because we have attached urgent priority to the training of the unemployed and to training in industry we are proposing to increase the

Vocational Training Assistance Act rates of contribution from the federal treasury-in this field. I make these remarks in commentary on the plea that was made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) for a national policy of technical and vocational training. The national framework is provided for in this act; the response is up to the province, exercising its own authority. In this field the federal government proposes; the provincial government disposes.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the legislation now before us, to amend the technical and vocational training act, is contrary to the educational system prevailing in Quebec.
I am, therefore, taking this opportunity to bring Quebec's claims to the minister's attention and explain the difference between the educational system in that province with regard to technical and vocational training compared with the other parts of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, among the main problems which labour circles are concerned with, unemployment in every form and job insecurity come first. To those problems may he added those created by automation, the training of our young people for work and the rehabilitation of the older workers who have been discharged as the result of new and advanced techniques.
It is currently said that this country and our province have known radical changes since the turn of the century, and that our economy, which was formerly centred on agriculture, has now become industrialized.
Within a few years, and more particularly following the economic development required by the war effort, and by developing the resource above and under ground, our country has become an industrial giant.
Amongst the chief problems we have to contend with in regard to automation, the primary one, in my opinion, is education, primary, secondary or university education as well as vocational training and adjustment. Everyone is aware that automation will require more engineers, more physicians, more mathematicians, more skilled machinists, more technicians of all sorts. It is certain that foremen will have to acquire more competence and that there will be new vocational qualifications required for the maintenance and repair trades. It is already a well-known fact

that our young people will be not be able to start their apprenticeship before having completed secondary education.
On the other hand, experience proves that the majority of teachers never worked in industry and that consequently they can hardly prepare young people to properly hold positions in industry. We are of the opinion that their academic level often leaves much to be desired, which is readily realized if one reads briefs submitted by teaching people. Hence teachers must have a better preparation and consequently it is extremely urgent to set up normal schools for technical training instructors, in order to emphasize quality as well as train a large enough teaching staff. Before being admitted to teach, teachers should spend two or three years in industry and should even be eligible for leave with pay to readjust themselves.
The training available at present in technical schools and technological institutes is complementary to primary and high school courses and is directly related to them through its academic requirements. Theoretical programs are devised so as to make pupils understand the whys and wherefores of everything, to instil principles and to give information. Practical courses are intended to make pupils understand the theoretical notions acquired in theory classes.
The so-called specialized training, at the outset, was devised to come to the rescue of young people who were leaving school prematurely for various reasons. Thus, Mr. Jean Delorme, the director of specialized training, could say that he had achieved his purpose when he had succeeded in securing for technical school students the equivalent of a ninth grade certificate.
The publicity given specialized training reveals, however, that such training is aimed at supplying "well trained operators", by technological schools, according to the leaflet on "specialized training" published under the signature of its general manager.
Having become what is called nowadays a technician, that is a graduate of a technological institute, is a starting point and not the ultimate end. According to the trade, it is only after a few years of post-graduate studies and practical experience supplied and gained in industry that the young man, after having tested his qualifications, will validly be able to consider himself a tradesman or a technician.
Too often, the public fancies that graduates who just completed their studies are experts in their specialties, that they can be full-fledged employees in their own right in industry and that they can give the same output as if they already had a few years' experience.
Vocational Training Assistance Act
Everyone knows that it is not so and that it will never be so, no matter how much the programs of the technological institutes are changed. Vocational training cannot be the exclusive responsibility of educational institutions. In fact, the latter can only provide basic training, since industry is the cornerstone of the whole system.
It follows that theoretical training is only a prerequisite to holding a job in a plant or on the site. It is on the job that one serves the apprenticeship that will permit one to become fully qualified in a particular trade.
In other words, theoretical training is nothing but an introduction to the apprenticeship which must be provided later, at the place of work, by the employer or the union.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to remind you that it is to apprenticeship that we owe the finest achievements both here and elsewhere: government buildings, bridges, dams, and numerous residential, industrial and business constructions which were carried out only through the efforts of a variety of trades and techniques.
Those men acquired their technical skill by serving their apprenticeship under skilled workers.
However, in view of the technical developments and the urgency of maximum production to meet competition, this formula has to be adapted constantly under conditions which are often difficult. That is why, at a certain moment, industry had to change its methods of production and go in for fractional production, chain production and exaggerated specialization with consequent loss of its traditional importance by apprenticeship.
In spite of everything, apprenticeship still has many advantages, namely a greater flexibility in adjusting to industrial needs and trade requirements. It provides an important part of sound learning by compelling the apprentice to live in the trade environment and working community in the factory, in the field or in the shop. As a result of the necessary physical and muscular effort, he acquires automatic movements required for the quick and sure performance of specialized work. It remains an important and reliable stage in the training of professional workers.
What is exactly a workshop school or a field school? Its purpose is to combine the practical training deemed essential to the practice of a trade and the theoretical instruction recognized as necessary to a full vocational training; to combine methods of teaching in order to make skilled workers better acquainted with the latest technical developments, thus enabling them to become genuine modern technicians; finally, to co-ordinate methods permitting and promoting in the

Vocational Training Assistance Act working environment theoretical instruction in keeping with the cultural needs of the workers.
Some industries try to bring about this coordination according to their needs and to the requirements of their output. They admit that without an active participation of industries to the setting up of true vocational training, it will be impossible to achieve worth-while results. In addition, as vocational training can only be developed in definite working conditions, it also implies the enlightened participation of unions.
Mr. Chairman, there is in Quebec the apprenticeship commission for vocational training. The immediate purpose of this legislation is to promote apprenticeship by the creation of commissions and vocational centres, through the co-operation of industrial and vocational groups and public authorities.
In our province, the expression "apprenticeship centre" generally refers to vocational training establishments directly under apprenticeship commissions.
The apprenticeship commission studies, develops and amends, as necessary, the theoretical and practical programs of each trade submitted by trade consulting committees and see that these programs are carried out.
The results of our apprenticeship system: in the industries, trades and crafts subject to an apprenticeship system, there was 30,727 apprentices divided among the following crafts, industries or services: barbers, hairdressers, commercial establishments, building industry, manufacturing industries, other industries and services.
Since training boards have been set up, the day and evening courses they provide have been taken by 48,521 apprentices and journeymen, as follows: automobile, 2,394; barbers and hairdressers, 4,620; construction, 31,484; footwear, 5,616; watchmaking, 175; printing, 4,232. Thus we see the important role played by the training boards which have been set up in the province of Quebec since the passage of the training assistance act in 1945.

speechtext: I will not argue as to the regularity of the amendment, which proposes to permit the federal government to make agreements with private institutions. It seems to me this measure can reach into the activities of private institutions in any province through agreements which the Minister of Labour and the federal government might make with the provinces themselves. In this way we are respecting the integrity of the provinces by making the agreements directly with them. I am afraid the amendment cannot be accepted.

speechtext: I have with some reluctance refrained from making a major speech on this bill but I should like to ask one question on this final clause. We all know that the problem in vocational education is, as in other areas of the education field, the lack of coordination. This is a situation which arises to a great extent because our educational system is such as to foster individuality within the provinces. I wonder how far this council will go in developing a national perspective or a philosophy of education which meets the needs of our rapidly changing situation?
